/conditions/osteoarthritis.title: Osteoarthritis UK: Symptoms, Treatment & Exercises
/conditions/osteoarthritis.description: Osteoarthritis (OA) in the UK: how to recognise symptoms, when to see a GP, NICE-aligned treatment, exercises and diet — written for patients.
/conditions/osteoarthritis.question: What is osteoarthritis?
/conditions/osteoarthritis.answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis in the UK. It happens when protective cartilage on the ends of your bones wears down over time, most often in knees, hips, hands and spine. Symptoms include joint pain that worsens with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, swelling and reduced movement. It's manageable with exercise, weight control, and, when needed, medication or joint replacement.

faqs.q: Can osteoarthritis be reversed?
faqs.a: No, cartilage loss can't currently be reversed, but symptoms and progression can be significantly slowed with exercise, weight management and joint-friendly activity.

faqs.q: What's the best exercise for osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming) plus strength training around the affected joint. NICE recommends 30 minutes most days.

faqs.q: Does osteoarthritis show on an X-ray?
faqs.a: Yes — X-rays show joint space narrowing and bone spurs, though symptoms don't always match imaging severity.

faqs.q: When should I see a GP?
faqs.a: If joint pain limits daily activity, wakes you at night, or hasn't improved after 6 weeks of self-management, book a GP appointment.

/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Symptoms, Treatment & Flares (UK)
/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.description: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in the UK: early symptoms, GP referral, DMARDs, flares and self-care — a plain-English guide for patients.
/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.question: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.answer: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of your joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness — usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet). Early treatment with DMARDs (disease-modifying drugs) within 3 months of symptoms starting can prevent joint damage. It affects about 400,000 adults in the UK.

faqs.q: Is rheumatoid arthritis a disability?
faqs.a: It can qualify as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it substantially affects daily activities. Many people with RA are eligible for PIP.

faqs.q: What's the difference between OA and RA?
faqs.a: OA is wear-and-tear cartilage loss. RA is an autoimmune inflammatory disease. RA usually affects joints symmetrically and causes prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour).

faqs.q: Can diet help RA?
faqs.a: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in oily fish, olive oil and vegetables can reduce inflammatory markers. It doesn't replace DMARDs but supports overall control.

/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.title: Psoriatic Arthritis UK | Symptoms & Treatment
/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.description: UK guide to psoriatic arthritis: the link between psoriasis and joint inflammation, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and self-care.
/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.question: What is psoriatic arthritis?
/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.answer: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis that affects around 1 in 5 people with psoriasis. It causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness — often in fingers, toes, lower back or knees — plus nail changes and skin plaques. Early diagnosis and DMARDs or biologics prevent joint damage.

faqs.q: Can you have PsA without psoriasis?
faqs.a: Yes, about 15% of people develop joint symptoms before skin symptoms. Family history and nail pitting are clues.

faqs.q: Is psoriatic arthritis worse than rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Both can cause serious joint damage. PsA has more variable patterns; RA is usually more symmetrical. Outcomes depend on early treatment.

/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.title: Ankylosing Spondylitis (axSpA) | UK Guide
/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.description: UK guide to ankylosing spondylitis: inflammatory back pain, morning stiffness, diagnosis, daily exercise, physio and biologic treatment.
/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.question: What is ankylosing spondylitis?
/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.answer: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), or axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory arthritis mainly affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints. It typically starts in the late teens or twenties with gradual lower back pain and morning stiffness that improves with movement. Daily exercise, physio and biologic drugs keep the spine flexible.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ankylosing spondylitis and axial spondyloarthritis?
faqs.a: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is the umbrella term. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the form of axSpA where damage to the sacroiliac joints is visible on an X-ray. Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) is the same condition earlier in its course — visible only on MRI. Treatment is the same for both.

faqs.q: What is the first sign of ankylosing spondylitis?
faqs.a: The earliest sign is usually persistent lower back or buttock pain that comes on slowly before age 45, is worse in the morning, lasts over 30 minutes and improves with movement.

faqs.q: Is ankylosing spondylitis a disability?
faqs.a: AS is recognised under the UK Equality Act 2010 as it can have a long-term substantial effect on daily activities. Many people qualify for reasonable adjustments at work and may be eligible for PIP.

faqs.q: Can ankylosing spondylitis be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but biologics, NSAIDs and daily exercise can keep inflammation under control and prevent spinal damage for most people.

faqs.q: What is the HLA-B27 test?
faqs.a: A blood test that checks for the HLA-B27 gene, found in around 90% of UK people with AS. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose AS — it's used alongside symptoms and MRI scans.

faqs.q: Should I exercise if my back hurts?
faqs.a: Yes — gentle, regular movement is the single most important treatment for AS. Pain that eases with activity is typical. A physiotherapist can build a safe, progressive programme.

/conditions/gout.title: Gout: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/gout.description: UK guide to gout: uric acid crystals, sudden severe joint pain, allopurinol treatment after repeat attacks, diet and alcohol changes.
/conditions/gout.question: What is gout?
/conditions/gout.answer: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by high uric acid crystallising inside joints — usually the big toe — triggering sudden severe pain, redness and swelling. UK guidelines recommend urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) after a second attack to prevent joint damage. Diet and alcohol adjustments help.

faqs.q: What are the first signs of gout?
faqs.a: The first sign is usually a sudden, severe attack of pain in a single joint — most often the big toe — that wakes you up at night. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and so tender that even the weight of a bedsheet feels unbearable. Attacks typically peak within 24 hours.

faqs.q: How do I know if my toe pain is gout?
faqs.a: Gout in the big toe (called podagra) comes on suddenly, usually overnight, with intense burning pain, redness, heat and swelling at the base of the toe. If you can't bear weight on it or even touch it, and the attack settles over 3–10 days, gout is the most likely cause. A blood test for uric acid and joint fluid analysis can confirm it.

faqs.q: What does a gout attack feel like?
faqs.a: Most people describe a sudden, intense burning or throbbing pain in one joint — often the big toe — that starts overnight. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and so tender that even a bedsheet can be unbearable.

faqs.q: Is gout curable?
faqs.a: Gout itself is a long-term condition, but with allopurinol or febuxostat plus diet and lifestyle changes, most people stop having attacks completely.

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid with gout?
faqs.a: Limit red meat, organ meats, shellfish, oily fish (anchovies, sardines), beer, spirits and sugary drinks. Cherries, water and low-fat dairy can help reduce attacks.

faqs.q: How long does a gout attack last?
faqs.a: An untreated attack peaks at 24 hours and usually settles within 3 to 10 days. NSAIDs or colchicine started early can shorten and ease attacks.

faqs.q: Is gout the same as arthritis?
faqs.a: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by uric-acid crystals, distinct from osteoarthritis (wear and tear) or rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune).

/conditions/fibromyalgia.title: Fibromyalgia: Symptoms & Management | UK Guide
/conditions/fibromyalgia.description: UK guide to fibromyalgia: widespread pain, fatigue, fibro fog and sleep problems, plus NICE-recommended exercise, CBT and pacing.
/conditions/fibromyalgia.question: What is fibromyalgia?
/conditions/fibromyalgia.answer: Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition causing widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and 'fibro fog'. It's a disorder of pain processing rather than joint damage. NICE recommends graded exercise, CBT and paced activity as first-line management.

faqs.q: Is fibromyalgia a form of arthritis?
faqs.a: No. Fibromyalgia doesn't damage joints or cause inflammation. However, it commonly occurs alongside arthritis and is treated by similar rheumatology teams.

faqs.q: How is fibromyalgia diagnosed in the UK?
faqs.a: Diagnosis is clinical — based on widespread pain lasting over 3 months, plus fatigue, sleep and cognitive symptoms. Blood tests are used to rule out other conditions.

faqs.q: What is fibro fog?
faqs.a: Fibro fog is the cognitive symptom of fibromyalgia — short-term memory lapses, word-finding difficulties and trouble concentrating. It improves with better sleep, pacing and exercise.

faqs.q: Can fibromyalgia be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but with self-management, exercise, medication and CBT, many people significantly reduce symptoms and stay in work and family life.

faqs.q: Does fibromyalgia get worse over time?
faqs.a: Fibromyalgia is not progressive — it doesn't damage tissue. Symptoms fluctuate, often worsening with stress, poor sleep or overdoing activity, and easing with steady self-management.

/conditions/lupus.title: Lupus (SLE): Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/lupus.description: UK guide to lupus (SLE): joint pain, butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity, plus hydroxychloroquine treatment and self-care.
/conditions/lupus.question: What is lupus?
/conditions/lupus.answer: Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, heart and lungs. Common symptoms include joint pain, a butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity. Hydroxychloroquine is the mainstay of treatment.

faqs.q: Is lupus a form of arthritis?
faqs.a: Lupus isn't classed as arthritis but it commonly causes joint pain and stiffness. Many people are managed by the same rheumatology teams that treat rheumatoid arthritis.

faqs.q: Can lupus be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but modern treatments — particularly hydroxychloroquine — control symptoms and reduce flares for most people. Many achieve long periods of remission.

faqs.q: What is the butterfly rash?
faqs.a: A flat or slightly raised red rash across the cheeks and bridge of the nose, in the shape of a butterfly. It is one of the most recognisable signs of lupus, though not everyone develops it.

faqs.q: Why is sun protection so important with lupus?
faqs.a: UV light can trigger lupus flares — both skin rashes and internal symptoms. Daily SPF 50, UV-protective clothing and hats are essential, even on cloudy UK days.

faqs.q: Can people with lupus have children?
faqs.a: Yes. Pregnancy in lupus needs to be planned with your rheumatology and obstetric team, ideally during a period of stable disease, with medications reviewed in advance.

/conditions/knee-arthritis.title: Knee Arthritis UK | Symptoms, Treatment & Exercises
/conditions/knee-arthritis.description: Knee arthritis symptoms, treatment & exercises: Pain relief strategies, exercises & when to see a specialist. Complete management guide.
/conditions/knee-arthritis.question: What is knee arthritis?
/conditions/knee-arthritis.answer: Knee arthritis is joint damage in the knee — most often osteoarthritis — causing pain when standing, walking or climbing stairs, stiffness after rest, and swelling. NICE recommends exercise and weight loss as first-line treatment; every 5 kg lost cuts knee load by roughly 20 kg.

faqs.q: What's the best exercise for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Quadriceps strengthening (straight-leg raises, wall sits) plus low-impact aerobic (cycling, swimming). 3-5 sessions a week for 8+ weeks shows meaningful pain reduction.

faqs.q: Should I use a walking stick?
faqs.a: Use it in the opposite hand to the painful knee — this reduces load by up to 25%.

/conditions/hip-arthritis.title: Hip Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
/conditions/hip-arthritis.description: UK guide to hip arthritis: groin and buttock pain, stiffness, physio-led strengthening, weight management and hip replacement options.
/conditions/hip-arthritis.question: What is hip arthritis?
/conditions/hip-arthritis.answer: Hip arthritis is joint damage — usually osteoarthritis — of the hip, causing groin or buttock pain, stiffness and difficulty putting on socks or shoes. Physio-led strengthening, weight management and, when severe, hip replacement (over 100,000 done in the UK each year) provide long-term relief.

faqs.q: What does hip arthritis feel like?
faqs.a: Most people feel a deep ache in the groin or front of the hip that worsens with walking, standing up from a chair, or putting on socks. Stiffness is common after sitting and first thing in the morning, usually easing within 30 minutes of moving.

faqs.q: How do I relieve hip pain while sleeping?
faqs.a: Sleep on your back or on the unaffected side with a firm pillow between your knees to keep the hips aligned. A medium-firm mattress, a warm bath before bed, and a topical NSAID gel applied to the hip help reduce night pain. Avoid sleeping on the painful side and don't tuck your top knee in front of the bottom one — it twists the joint.

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for hip arthritis?
faqs.a: Glute and hip-abductor strengthening (bridges, clams, side-lying leg raises) combined with low-impact cardio such as cycling, swimming or pool walking is the most evidence-based approach. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for everyone with hip OA.

faqs.q: Should I keep walking with hip arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. Regular walking strengthens the muscles that support the hip and reduces pain over time. Build up gradually, wear cushioned shoes, and use a walking pole in the hand opposite to the painful hip to offload the joint by up to 25%.

faqs.q: When is a hip replacement needed?
faqs.a: Hip replacement is usually considered when pain disturbs sleep, severely limits walking or daily activity, and conservative measures (exercise, weight management, painkillers, injections) have not worked over several months. UK outcomes are excellent — over 95% of hip replacements still function well at 10 years.

faqs.q: Does losing weight help hip arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. The hip carries roughly three times body weight when walking and up to five times when climbing stairs, so even small weight loss meaningfully reduces joint load and pain.

/conditions/hand-arthritis.title: Hand Arthritis UK | Symptoms, Treatment & Exercises
/conditions/hand-arthritis.description: Hand arthritis: Symptoms, functional strategies & adaptive equipment. Maintain independence with expert physiotherapy & practical aids.
/conditions/hand-arthritis.question: What is hand arthritis?
/conditions/hand-arthritis.answer: Hand arthritis affects the small joints of the fingers, thumbs and wrists. Osteoarthritis typically causes bony bumps and thumb-base pain; rheumatoid usually causes symmetrical knuckle swelling. Splints, hand exercises and topical NSAID gels help most people.

faqs.q: What are the first signs of hand arthritis?
faqs.a: Early signs include stiffness in the fingers in the morning, a dull ache at the base of the thumb when opening jars or turning keys, and small bony lumps on the end finger joints (Heberden's nodes).

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for arthritic hands?
faqs.a: A daily 5-minute routine of fist-to-fan, finger-to-thumb touches, and gentle putty squeezes maintains range of motion and grip strength without overloading inflamed joints.

faqs.q: Do hand splints actually help?
faqs.a: Yes — for thumb base (CMC) arthritis, a custom or off-the-shelf neoprene splint reduces pain during pinching tasks and is recommended by NICE as part of first-line care.

faqs.q: Are the bony lumps on my fingers permanent?
faqs.a: Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes are bone changes and don't shrink, but the pain associated with their formation usually settles within 1–2 years. The remaining stiffness can be managed with exercise.

faqs.q: When is hand surgery needed?
faqs.a: Surgery (most commonly trapeziectomy for thumb base arthritis or joint fusion for severe finger OA) is reserved for persistent pain that hasn't responded to splinting, exercise, injections and topical NSAIDs over 6+ months.

/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.title: Shoulder Arthritis UK | Symptoms & Exercises
/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.description: UK guide to shoulder arthritis: glenohumeral & AC joint OA, rotator cuff arthropathy, symptoms, treatment and exercises.
/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.question: What is shoulder arthritis?
/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.answer: Shoulder arthritis is cartilage loss in the glenohumeral or acromioclavicular joints, causing deep aching pain, reduced reach and night pain when lying on the affected side. Physio, corticosteroid injections and, if severe, shoulder replacement are options.

faqs.q: What does shoulder arthritis feel like?
faqs.a: Most people describe a deep ache at the back of the shoulder that worsens when reaching overhead, behind the back, or lying on that side at night. Stiffness limits putting on coats and reaching seatbelts.

faqs.q: Is shoulder arthritis the same as a frozen shoulder?
faqs.a: No. Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is inflammation of the joint capsule and usually resolves within 1–3 years. Shoulder arthritis is cartilage wear and is progressive — but both can cause similar early symptoms, so accurate diagnosis matters.

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for shoulder arthritis?
faqs.a: Pendulum swings, doorway stretches and gentle external rotation with a resistance band are the most evidence-supported exercises. They protect range of motion and rotator cuff strength without overloading the joint.

faqs.q: Should I get an injection in my shoulder?
faqs.a: Corticosteroid injections can give 6–12 weeks of meaningful pain relief and are useful to bridge a flare or to allow physiotherapy to progress. Most clinicians limit injections to 2–3 per year.

faqs.q: When is shoulder replacement needed?
faqs.a: Shoulder replacement is considered when night pain is severe, function is limited despite physiotherapy and injections, and X-rays confirm advanced joint changes. The reverse total shoulder replacement is the most common option in the UK.

/conditions/elbow-arthritis.title: Elbow Arthritis UK | Causes, Treatment & Exercises
/conditions/elbow-arthritis.description: UK guide to elbow pain and arthritis: causes of elbow joint pain, tennis and golfer's elbow, osteoarthritis, the best gentle exercises and when to see a GP.
/conditions/elbow-arthritis.question: What is elbow arthritis?
/conditions/elbow-arthritis.answer: Elbow arthritis is joint damage in the elbow causing pain, stiffness, locking or grating during movement. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are the main causes. Treatment ranges from activity modification and NSAIDs to arthroscopy or elbow replacement.

faqs.q: What does elbow arthritis feel like?
faqs.a: Most people describe a deep ache on the outside or back of the elbow that worsens when straightening the arm fully or carrying a heavy bag. Many lose the last few degrees of extension, so the arm no longer goes completely straight.

faqs.q: Is elbow pain always arthritis?
faqs.a: No. The most common causes of elbow pain in UK adults are tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) and golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis) — tendon overload conditions rather than joint arthritis. True elbow arthritis is less common and usually follows an old fracture or develops in people with rheumatoid arthritis.

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for elbow arthritis?
faqs.a: Gentle range-of-motion work — bending and straightening the elbow within a pain-free range, plus forearm rotations (palm up, palm down) — is the most evidence-supported routine. Light isometric grip work protects forearm strength without loading the joint.

faqs.q: Should I see a GP about elbow pain?
faqs.a: See your GP if elbow pain lasts more than six weeks, wakes you at night, locks or catches, or is accompanied by tingling into the ring and little fingers — that pattern can indicate ulnar nerve irritation that benefits from early treatment.

faqs.q: Can elbow arthritis be cured?
faqs.a: Arthritis itself isn't cured, but most people manage symptoms well with exercise, activity modification, topical NSAIDs and occasional corticosteroid injections. Elbow replacement is reserved for severe pain or loss of function and gives good relief in around 85% of cases.

/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.title: Juvenile Arthritis (JIA) in Children | UK Guide
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.description: UK guide to juvenile idiopathic arthritis: signs in children under 16, diagnosis, paediatric rheumatology care and DMARD treatment.
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.question: What is juvenile arthritis?
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.answer: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is arthritis starting before age 16, lasting more than 6 weeks. It affects around 1 in 1,000 UK children. Early paediatric rheumatology care and DMARDs help most children live active lives.

faqs.q: What are the first signs of arthritis in a child?
faqs.a: Look out for limping (worse in the morning), a swollen joint, a child avoiding a normally favourite activity, or unexplained fevers and rashes. Always see your GP if joint symptoms last more than two weeks.

faqs.q: Is juvenile arthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: No. JIA is its own group of conditions. Some forms behave similarly to rheumatoid arthritis, but JIA also includes types not seen in adults, such as systemic JIA (Still's disease).

faqs.q: Will my child grow out of JIA?
faqs.a: Some children — particularly those with oligoarticular JIA — do go into long-term remission. Others have ongoing disease into adulthood. Modern treatments have transformed the outlook for most.

faqs.q: Why does my child need eye checks?
faqs.a: JIA can cause silent eye inflammation (uveitis) that, if missed, can damage sight. Regular slit-lamp checks by an ophthalmologist are essential.

faqs.q: Can my child still play sport?
faqs.a: Yes — sport is encouraged. Swimming and cycling are particularly good. Adapt during flares and work with the rheumatology team and PE staff.

/conditions/reactive-arthritis.title: Reactive Arthritis: Causes & Recovery | UK Guide
/conditions/reactive-arthritis.description: UK guide to reactive arthritis: joint inflammation after gut or urinary infection, typical symptoms, treatment and recovery timeline.
/conditions/reactive-arthritis.question: What is reactive arthritis?
/conditions/reactive-arthritis.answer: Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body — usually gut or urinary. Symptoms include joint pain, eye inflammation and urinary symptoms. Most cases resolve within 3-12 months.

faqs.q: How long does reactive arthritis last?
faqs.a: Most people recover fully within 3 to 6 months. Around 1 in 5 develop longer-lasting joint problems, and a smaller number go on to develop a chronic inflammatory arthritis, which is why early specialist input matters.

faqs.q: Is reactive arthritis curable?
faqs.a: Yes — for most people reactive arthritis settles completely once the triggering infection clears and inflammation is treated. NSAIDs, joint injections and physiotherapy speed recovery.

faqs.q: Can reactive arthritis come back?
faqs.a: It can. People with the HLA-B27 gene are more likely to have repeat episodes, often triggered by a new gut or urinary infection. Practising food hygiene and safer sex reduces the risk.

faqs.q: How is reactive arthritis diagnosed in the UK?
faqs.a: Your GP will ask about recent gut, urinary or chest infections and examine your joints, eyes and skin. Blood tests (CRP, ESR, HLA-B27), urine tests and sometimes joint fluid analysis or imaging are used to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other arthritis.

faqs.q: Is reactive arthritis contagious?
faqs.a: No. Reactive arthritis itself cannot be passed from person to person. However, the infections that trigger it (such as chlamydia or salmonella) can be — so treating partners and practising good food hygiene matters.

faqs.q: What is the difference between reactive arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Reactive arthritis is triggered by a recent infection, usually affects one or a few large joints, and most people recover within months. Rheumatoid arthritis is a lifelong autoimmune disease that typically affects small joints on both sides of the body and needs long-term medication.

/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) | UK Guide
/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.description: UK guide to polymyalgia rheumatica: sudden shoulder and hip stiffness over 50, low-dose steroid treatment and what recovery looks like.
/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.question: What is polymyalgia rheumatica?
/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.answer: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) causes sudden shoulder and hip stiffness and pain, mainly in adults over 50. Low-dose steroids (prednisolone 15 mg) usually give dramatic relief within days. Treatment typically continues for 1-2 years.

faqs.q: How is polymyalgia rheumatica diagnosed in the UK?
faqs.a: Your GP will check your symptoms, examine your shoulders and hips, and arrange blood tests (CRP and ESR) to look for inflammation. A dramatic improvement within a few days of starting prednisolone helps confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: How long does polymyalgia rheumatica last?
faqs.a: Most people need steroid treatment for 1 to 3 years. Around half of those affected have one or more flares during the taper, but the condition usually goes into long-term remission.

faqs.q: Is polymyalgia rheumatica an autoimmune disease?
faqs.a: Yes — PMR is driven by an overactive immune response that inflames the lining of joints and bursae, particularly in the shoulders and hips. It is not contagious and is not caused by anything you have done.

faqs.q: What is the link with giant cell arteritis?
faqs.a: Around 1 in 5 people with PMR also develop giant cell arteritis (GCA), which inflames blood vessels in the head. New headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, or any change in vision need urgent medical attention.

faqs.q: Can I exercise with polymyalgia rheumatica?
faqs.a: Yes, and you should. Gentle walking, shoulder and hip mobility work, and light resistance training protect muscle and bone during long-term steroid use. Start slowly and build up.

faqs.q: Are there natural alternatives to steroids for PMR?
faqs.a: There is no proven natural alternative to steroids for PMR — untreated inflammation can damage tissue and increase the risk of GCA. A Mediterranean diet, exercise and bone-protection medicines support steroid treatment rather than replace it.

/guides/newly-diagnosed.title: Newly Diagnosed With Arthritis: UK First Steps Checklist
/guides/newly-diagnosed.description: Newly diagnosed with arthritis in the UK? Find first steps, questions for your GP, rheumatology preparation and guides to pain, exercise, diet and benefits.
/guides/newly-diagnosed.question: What should I do after an arthritis diagnosis?
/guides/newly-diagnosed.answer: Learn which type you have, keep gentle daily movement, write questions for your GP or rheumatology appointment, and track symptoms. Then explore pain relief, exercise, diet and benefits if daily living is limited. Educational guidance, not a diagnosis.

faqs.q: Iâve just been diagnosed â what should I do first?
faqs.a: Get a copy of your diagnosis letter, confirm exactly which type of arthritis you have, write down your top 3 questions, and book a follow-up so you have someone to ask as new questions come up. Donât rush major treatment decisions in the first week.

faqs.q: Will I become disabled?
faqs.a: Most people with arthritis stay independent throughout their lives with the right treatment. Outcomes have improved dramatically over the last 20 years thanks to earlier diagnosis, better medications, and stronger evidence for exercise and self-management.

faqs.q: Should I stop exercising?
faqs.a: No â almost the opposite. Appropriate exercise is one of the most effective treatments for arthritis. Start gently (walking, swimming, tai chi), build slowly, and work with a physiotherapist if youâre unsure where to begin.

faqs.q: Is arthritis hereditary?
faqs.a: Genetics influences risk for several types of arthritis (especially rheumatoid and ankylosing spondylitis), but isnât the whole story. Lifestyle, weight, joint injuries and environment all play significant roles.

faqs.q: Can I still work?
faqs.a: Yes â most people with arthritis continue working. You have legal protection under the Equality Act 2010, including the right to reasonable adjustments. See our work-and-arthritis guide for details.

faqs.q: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.a: A Mediterranean-style diet has the strongest evidence for arthritis â plenty of vegetables, oily fish, olive oil, nuts and whole grains, with less red meat and processed food. There is no single magic food, but the overall pattern matters.

faqs.q: What about supplements?
faqs.a: Some supplements (omega-3, turmeric/curcumin, vitamin D if deficient) have modest evidence. Glucosamine and chondroitin have mixed results. Always tell your prescriber before starting â several interact with arthritis medications.

faqs.q: When should I call my team between appointments?
faqs.a: Contact them for: a sudden severe flare; signs of infection (fever, redness, swelling); new neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness); concerning medication side effects; or major mental health distress. Donât wait if something feels wrong.

faqs.q: Can I claim any benefits?
faqs.a: If arthritis significantly affects daily living or mobility, you may qualify for Personal Independence Payment (PIP). The claim is based on functional impact, not diagnosis. See our PIP guide for the step-by-step process.

faqs.q: How do I find other people with arthritis?
faqs.a: Our free Connect Groups are facilitated peer communities â online and in-person, by condition or life stage. Sharing the experience with people who get it makes a real difference to wellbeing and outcomes.

/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.title: Arthritis Pain Relief UK: Movement, Heat & Medicines
/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.description: Practical UK arthritis pain relief: paced movement, heat and cold, topical treatments, sleep and when to contact your GP. Find next steps for self-care.
/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.question: How do I relieve arthritis pain today?
/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.answer: Start with paced movement, heat or cold on the joint, and a topical NSAID gel if suitable. Protect sleep and see your GP if pain lasts more than six weeks, a joint is hot and swollen, or night pain wakes you. Educational guidance, not a diagnosis.

/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.title: Best Hip Exercises for Osteoarthritis | UK Guide
/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.description: Evidence-based hip OA exercises: glute bridges, clamshells, hip abduction, wall squats and cycling — with NICE-aligned weekly targets.
/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.question: What are the best hip exercises for osteoarthritis?
/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.answer: Evidence-based hip OA exercises include glute bridges, clamshells, standing hip abduction, wall squats and stationary cycling. Aim for 3 sessions per week of 30 minutes; expect meaningful pain reduction after 8-12 weeks. NICE guideline NG226 recommends supervised programmes.

/guides/knee-exercises-for-osteoarthriti.title: Free Knee Exercises for Osteoarthritis UK | 8-Move Home Routine
/guides/knee-exercises-for-osteoarthriti.description: Free NICE-aligned knee exercises for osteoarthritis in the UK — eight home moves, weekly plan, 4/10 pain rule, red flags and FAQs. Living With Arthritis charity 1218461.
/guides/knee-exercises-for-osteoarthriti.question: What are the best free knee exercises for osteoarthritis in the UK?
/guides/knee-exercises-for-osteoarthriti.answer: NICE NG226 recommends structured exercise as first-line for knee osteoarthritis. A practical home routine includes quad sets, straight-leg raises, sit-to-stands, mini squats, step-ups, hamstring curls, calf raises and gentle range-of-motion — 2–3 sessions weekly with a 4/10 pain rule.

faqs.q: How many reps should I do?
faqs.a: Typically 2–3 sets of 8–12 reps, two to three times a week on non-consecutive days. Progress by about 10% per week.

faqs.q: When should I stop?
faqs.a: Stop if pain is sharp, catching, or stays above about 4/10 overnight. Mild ache that settles within 24 hours is usually fine.

faqs.q: Can I start while waiting for NHS physio?
faqs.a: Yes for most stable knee OA — begin gently at home and ask about MSK self-referral. Seek urgent care for red-flag symptoms.

/guides/free-arthritis-resources-uk.title: Free Arthritis Resources UK | Living With Arthritis Charity Guides & Tools
/guides/free-arthritis-resources-uk.description: Free UK arthritis resources from Living With Arthritis (charity 1218461): home physio exercises, diet advice, PIP claim tools and newly diagnosed checklists. Independent of Arthritis UK.
/guides/free-arthritis-resources-uk.question: What free arthritis resources do UK charities offer?
/guides/free-arthritis-resources-uk.answer: Living With Arthritis (charity 1218461) offers free home exercise routines, diet advice, PIP claim tools and newly diagnosed checklists. Arthritis UK and NRAS also provide free information. Living With Arthritis is independent of Arthritis UK.

faqs.q: Is Living With Arthritis the same as Arthritis UK?
faqs.a: No — it is an independent UK charity (1218461), not Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis).

faqs.q: Are the exercise and PIP tools free?
faqs.a: Yes. Guides, home physio routines, the PIP evidence diary and flare plan are free to use.

/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.title: Can Exercise Make Osteoarthritis Worse? | UK Guide
/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.description: Worried exercise will damage arthritic joints? What normal soreness looks like, warning signs of overdoing it, and how to progress safely.
/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.question: Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse?
/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.answer: No — done correctly, exercise reduces OA pain and slows progression. Some soreness during and up to 2 hours after exercise is normal. Sharp, sudden or persistent pain lasting more than 24 hours means you've done too much; scale back but don't stop.

/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.title: Fall Prevention with Arthritis | UK Strength & Balance
/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.description: UK fall prevention with arthritis: strength and balance exercises, a home safety checklist, medication review and practical steps to take after a fall.
/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.question: How can older adults prevent falls?
/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.answer: Strength and balance training (tai chi, Otago programme) cuts falls by around 30%. Also: home hazard checks, medication review, eye tests every 2 years and vitamin D 10 mcg/day. Contact your GP or NHS falls clinic if you've fallen twice in a year.

/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.title: Sarcopenia: Rebuilding Muscle After 60 | UK Guide
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.description: UK guide to sarcopenia: why age-related muscle loss worsens arthritis, and how resistance training and protein intake can reverse it.
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.question: What is sarcopenia?
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.answer: Sarcopenia is age-related muscle loss that accelerates after 60 and worsens arthritis symptoms. Resistance training (2-3 sessions per week) plus 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day reverses much of it, even in your 80s.
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.bodyHtml:
What is sarcopenia and why arthritis speeds it up

Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of muscle mass, strength and function that typically accelerates after age 60. Arthritis speeds it up because pain and stiffness reduce daily movement, so muscles around painful joints waste faster than in active peers. Weak muscles then load joints harder — a loop that worsens both problems.

Protein targets that support muscle

Many older adults in the UK eat too little protein across the day. A practical target is about 1.0–1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight daily, spread over meals, unless a clinician has set a different plan (for example kidney disease). Dairy, eggs, fish, lean meat, tofu and fortified drinks all count. Pair protein with resistance work — food alone rarely reverses sarcopenia.

Home checks that raise a flag

Simple signs include a slower usual walking pace, weaker grip, needing both hands to rise from a chair, or unintentional weight loss. These are not a diagnosis, but they are a reason to talk to your GP about strength, falls risk and whether a formal assessment or physiotherapy referral helps.

Strength training adapted for arthritis

Two to three short sessions a week of sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, resistance-band rows and heel raises usually beat long cardio alone for muscle. Stay below sharp joint pain; mild muscle ache the next day is normal. If a joint is hot and swollen, switch to gentle range-of-motion until the flare settles.

Supplements — what has evidence

Vitamin D (especially in UK winter), creatine and leucine-rich protein have the best support when combined with training. Supplements without strength work rarely rebuild muscle. Check with a pharmacist or GP before starting creatine or high-dose vitamin D if you take other medicines.

/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.title: Improving Bone Density & Osteoporosis | UK Guide
/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.description: How to improve bone density in the UK: weight-bearing exercise, resistance training, calcium and vitamin D, FRAX scores and treatment.
/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.question: How do I improve bone density?
/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.answer: Weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing), resistance training, calcium 700 mg/day and vitamin D 10 mcg/day support bone density. If your FRAX score is high, your GP may prescribe bisphosphonates.

/guides/disability-support.title: Your Disability Rights With Arthritis: Equality Act 2010
/guides/disability-support.description: Your UK disability rights with arthritis: when it counts as a disability, discrimination types, reasonable adjustments at work and in services, what to do.
/guides/disability-support.question: What are my disability rights in the UK if I have arthritis?
/guides/disability-support.answer: Under the Equality Act 2010 (England, Scotland and Wales), arthritis counts as a disability if it has a substantial and long-term negative effect on your normal daily activities. If it does, employers, shops, services, schools, colleges and landlords must not discriminate against you, and many must make reasonable adjustments. Northern Ireland has similar protection under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995.
/guides/disability-support.bodyHtml:
Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010, GOV.UK: Disability rights and the Equality Act 2010 on legislation.gov.uk. This is general information, not legal advice.

Many people with arthritis do not think of themselves as disabled. But in law, "disabled" is not about using a wheelchair or looking unwell. It is about the effect your condition has on everyday life. If your arthritis meets the legal definition, you have real, enforceable rights at work, in shops and services, in education and in housing. This guide explains those rights in plain English, and what to do if they are not respected.

Does arthritis count as a disability?

GOV.UK says you are disabled under the Equality Act 2010 if you have a physical or mental impairment that has a substantial and long-term negative effect on your ability to do normal daily activities.

TermWhat it meansArthritis examples
SubstantialMore than minor or trivial. GOV.UK's example is a daily task like getting dressed taking much longer than usual.Needing much longer to dress, struggling with buttons, jars or taps, being unable to walk far or stand for long
Long-termHas lasted, or is likely to last, at least 12 months, or for the rest of your lifeOsteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis and gout with ongoing effects
Normal daily activitiesEveryday things such as walking, dressing, washing, cooking, shopping, using a keyboard or travellingGripping, carrying shopping, climbing stairs, getting in and out of a car

Flares and fluctuating arthritis

GOV.UK specifically mentions arthritis as an example of a recurring or fluctuating condition, which has special rules. Under Schedule 1 of the Act, if an impairment stops having a substantial effect but that effect is likely to recur, it is treated as continuing. So if your arthritis flares and settles, the good weeks do not stop you being protected.

The effect of treatment

Schedule 1 also says that if measures, including medical treatment and aids, are being taken to treat or correct an impairment, you look at the effect it would be likely to have without them. In practice, this means arthritis that is well controlled by medicines such as DMARDs or biologics can still count as a disability, because of its likely effect without treatment.

Only a court or tribunal can decide for certain whether you are disabled in law. Keeping records of how arthritis affects you, and letters from your healthcare team, helps if this is ever questioned.

The types of disability discrimination

TypeWhat it meansExample
Direct discriminationTreating you less favourably because you are disabledNot being offered a job because the employer assumes people with arthritis take a lot of time off
Discrimination arising from disabilityTreating you unfavourably because of something connected with your disability, unless it can be justified as a proportionate way of achieving a legitimate aimA warning for absences caused by flares, or for being slower at a task because of hand pain
Indirect discriminationA rule that applies to everyone but puts disabled people at an unfair disadvantage, unless it can be justifiedA rule that everyone must start at 7am, when morning stiffness makes this very hard
Failure to make reasonable adjustmentsNot taking reasonable steps to remove a disadvantageRefusing a suitable chair or keyboard without good reason
HarassmentUnwanted behaviour linked to disability that violates your dignity or creates an offensive environmentRepeated jokes about how slowly you walk
VictimisationTreating you unfairly because you complained about discrimination or supported someone else's complaintBeing left out of training after raising a grievance

Discrimination arising from disability does not apply if the person did not know, and could not reasonably have been expected to know, about your disability. This is one reason why telling an employer or service about your arthritis can help.

GOV.UK says you are also protected if you are associated with a disabled person, for example as their carer or parent.

Reasonable adjustments: the key right

Section 20 of the Act describes three requirements. Where the duty applies, an organisation must take reasonable steps to avoid a substantial disadvantage caused by:

  1. a provision, criterion or practice, such as a policy or way of doing things
  2. a physical feature, such as steps or heavy doors
  3. the lack of an auxiliary aid, such as equipment or a service

Where information is involved, reasonable steps include providing it in an accessible format. Importantly, section 20 says the organisation cannot normally charge you for the cost of making the adjustment.

Your rights at work

GOV.UK says the Act covers application forms, interviews, aptitude tests, job offers, terms of employment including pay, promotion, transfer and training, discipline and grievances, and dismissal or redundancy. Employers must make reasonable adjustments for disabled employees and job applicants. GOV.UK's own example of an adjustment is a special keyboard for someone with arthritis.

During recruitment, an employer can usually only ask about your health for limited reasons, such as whether you can do a task that is essential to the job or whether you need adjustments for the interview.

Our working with arthritis toolkit explains how to use these rights, and our adjustment letter templates help you ask in writing. Access to Work can fund support beyond what your employer must provide.

Shops, services and public bodies

The Act protects you when you use goods, services and facilities, including shops, banks, restaurants, transport, GP surgeries and hospitals, councils and leisure centres. Service providers must not discriminate against you and must make reasonable adjustments. Examples for arthritis might include:

  • a seat while you wait, or being allowed to wait somewhere other than a queue
  • help carrying shopping, or assistance at a station or airport
  • an appointment at a time of day when your stiffness is better
  • information or forms you can complete by phone or online if writing is painful
  • accessible parking near the entrance

For parking concessions, see our Blue Badge guide.

Health and social care

GP surgeries, hospitals, pharmacies, dentists and care services are service providers too, so the duty to make reasonable adjustments applies. For people with arthritis, useful adjustments might include a ground-floor consulting room, a longer appointment if dressing and undressing takes time, a telephone or video appointment during a flare, a chair in the waiting area with arms to push up from, or medicines in easy-open containers if you ask for them. If you have a carer, the practice can note that on your record so they can help with appointments. Ask the practice manager if you are unsure who to speak to.

Education

GOV.UK says it is against the law for a school or other education provider to treat disabled students unfavourably, and education providers must make reasonable adjustments, such as extra support and aids. Universities and colleges should have someone responsible for disability support you can talk to. This can matter for young people with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and for adults studying or retraining.

Housing

The Act covers buying and renting land or property. Landlords and managing agents must not discriminate against you, and may have to make reasonable adjustments, such as changing a policy or term of the tenancy. They do not usually have to make physical changes to your home, but you can ask permission for adaptations, and a Disabled Facilities Grant or council support may help pay for them. See our financial help directory for adaptations funding.

Public bodies: the public sector equality duty

Section 149 of the Act puts an extra duty on public authorities, such as councils, NHS bodies, government departments and state schools. When carrying out their functions, they must have due regard to the need to eliminate discrimination, harassment and victimisation, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations. This does not give you a separate right to compensation, but it is useful to mention if a council or NHS body makes a decision or policy without thinking about how it affects disabled people.

How to ask a service for an adjustment

You do not need to quote the law, but it can help to be clear. A simple approach:

  1. Say that you have arthritis, which is a disability, and explain the specific difficulty: "I cannot stand in a queue for more than a few minutes because of my knees."
  2. Say what would help: "Could I wait in a seat and be called when it is my turn?"
  3. If the answer is no, ask politely what alternatives they can offer, and who you can speak to.
  4. Afterwards, write down what happened, and make a complaint in writing if needed, saying you asked for a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010 (or the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 in Northern Ireland).

Template: incident record

If you think you have been treated unfairly, a record made at the time is valuable. Copy this table and fill in a row for each incident.

Date and timeWhereWho was involvedWhat happened and what was saidWitnessesWhat I did next

Keep copies of emails, letters, policies and any medical evidence about how arthritis affects you. Note down your time limit as soon as something happens.

Northern Ireland

GOV.UK says the Equality Act 2010 does not apply to Northern Ireland. There, the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 gives similar protection, including a duty on employers to make reasonable adjustments. The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland gives free and confidential advice, and employment complaints go to an industrial tribunal.

What to do if your rights are not respected

  1. Raise it informally. Explain the problem calmly, mention that you have arthritis and that you are asking for a reasonable adjustment or fair treatment.
  2. Put it in writing. Keep copies, and record dates, names and what was said.
  3. Use the complaints or grievance procedure. Most employers, services and public bodies have one.
  4. Get advice. GOV.UK lists the Equality Advisory and Support Service, Disability Rights UK, Advicenow and Citizens Advice. Acas helps with work disputes in Great Britain. You may be able to get legal aid for discrimination cases through Civil Legal Advice if you are eligible.
  5. Know the time limits. GOV.UK says employment tribunal claims usually have to be made within 6 months of the problem, and you must contact Acas first. For goods, services, housing and education claims in the county court (or sheriff court in Scotland), section 118 of the Act sets a time limit of 6 months starting with the date of the act complained of, unless the court decides another period is just and equitable.

We are not connected to any of the organisations mentioned. They are listed because they offer free, independent help.

When to get medical help

Your rights do not depend on having a particular treatment, but your healthcare team can help by describing how arthritis affects you. Speak to your GP or rheumatology team if your symptoms are getting worse or stopping you doing everyday things. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever. If discrimination is affecting your mental health, talk to your GP.

/guides/frailty-management-hub.description: Managing frailty alongside arthritis: strength training, protein-rich diet, medication review, sensory checks and GP frailty assessment.
/guides/frailty-management-hub.question: How is frailty managed with arthritis?
/guides/frailty-management-hub.answer: Frailty and arthritis together respond to comprehensive geriatric assessment: strength training, protein-rich diet, medication review, hearing/vision checks and social connection. Ask your GP for a formal frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale) review.

/guides/preventative-msk-health.title: Preventative Muscle & Joint Health | UK Guide
/guides/preventative-msk-health.description: Keep muscles and joints healthy for life: weekly activity targets, strength sessions, sleep, Mediterranean diet and weight guidance.
/guides/preventative-msk-health.question: How do I keep my muscles and joints healthy?
/guides/preventative-msk-health.answer: The three pillars are: 150 minutes moderate aerobic activity per week, 2 strength sessions per week, and 7-9 hours of sleep. Add Mediterranean-style diet, don't smoke, and keep BMI under 27 for lowest lifetime arthritis risk.

/guides/musculoskeletal-health.title: Musculoskeletal Health Guide | Living With Arthritis
/guides/musculoskeletal-health.description: Understand musculoskeletal health: back and neck pain, common symptoms, workplace ergonomics, UK healthcare pathways and rehabilitation options.
/guides/musculoskeletal-health.question: What is musculoskeletal health?
/guides/musculoskeletal-health.answer: Musculoskeletal (MSK) health means healthy bones, joints, muscles, tendons and ligaments. MSK conditions affect 20 million people in the UK. Movement, strength, sleep and weight management are the four proven levers to protect it.

/diet-hub.title: Diet & Nutrition Hub for Arthritis | UK
/diet-hub.description: The best diet for arthritis: Mediterranean eating, anti-inflammatory foods, weight loss guidance and UK supermarket-friendly meal plans.
/diet-hub.question: What's the best diet for arthritis?
/diet-hub.answer: A Mediterranean diet — oily fish twice a week, olive oil, nuts, wholegrains, plenty of vegetables and fruit — consistently reduces inflammation markers and joint pain in trials. Cut ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks and excess red meat. Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain.

/exercise-hub.title: Free Arthritis Exercises at Home UK | Exercise Hub
/exercise-hub.description: Arthritis exercises: Joint-specific routines for knees, hands, hips, back. Low-impact, evidence-based programmes from an HCPC physiotherapist.
/exercise-hub.question: What's the best exercise for arthritis?
/exercise-hub.answer: Combine aerobic (walking, swimming, cycling) with strength training 2-3 times a week and flexibility work. NICE guideline NG226 recommends exercise as first-line for all arthritis types — with pain reduction comparable to NSAIDs and no side effects.

/arthritis-support/london.title: Arthritis Support in London | Free UK Guide
/arthritis-support/london.description: Free arthritis support for people in London: NHS physio self-referral, local rheumatology at London Rheumatology, NHS trusts across all boroughs, exercise classes, and benefits help.
/arthritis-support/london.question: Where can I find arthritis support in London?
/arthritis-support/london.answer: Living With Arthritis is a national charity supporting people with arthritis across the UK, including those in London and the surrounding area. If you live in London and are managing joint pain, our free, NICE-aligned guides on exercise, anti-inflammatory diet, pain relief and NHS self-referral routes are available online. For local NHS care, London is served by London Rheumatology, NHS trusts across all boroughs, which provides rheumatology and musculoskeletal (MSK) services — you can usually access physiotherapy through NHS self-referral without a GP appointment.

faqs.q: How do I access NHS physiotherapy in London?
faqs.a: Most parts of London allow direct self-referral to NHS MSK physiotherapy — search 'NHS physiotherapy self referral London' or ask your GP practice. Waiting times vary but are typically 4-12 weeks; our Exercise Hub offers evidence-based routines you can start immediately.

faqs.q: Are there free arthritis exercise classes in London?
faqs.a: London usually has options through NHS falls-prevention programmes, local council leisure schemes, Age UK, and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) groups. Search 'London strength and balance class' or 'London tai chi for arthritis' — your GP practice or local library often maintain lists. Our online Tai Chi hub is free and joint-friendly if travelling is difficult.

faqs.q: How do I claim PIP for arthritis if I live in London?
faqs.a: PIP claims work the same across England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland uses Adult Disability Payment). Your local Citizens Advice office in London offers free application help. Read our benefits guide for a step-by-step overview.

/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.title: Paracetamol vs Ibuprofen for Arthritis Pain
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.description: For arthritis pain in UK adults, NICE recommends topical NSAID gels (like ibuprofen gel) first for hand and knee OA. Oral paracetamol is a reasonable short-t...
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.breadcrumb: Paracetamol vs Ibuprofen for Arthritis Pain
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.question: Should I take paracetamol or ibuprofen for arthritis pain?
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.answer: For arthritis pain in UK adults, NICE recommends topical NSAID gels (like ibuprofen gel) first for hand and knee OA. Oral paracetamol is a reasonable short-term option but the evidence for its benefit in OA is weaker than once thought. Oral ibuprofen works better for inflammation but carries stomach, kidney and heart risks — take it with food, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, and check with your GP if you're over 65, on blood pressure medication, or have kidney or heart conditions.

faqs.q: When would you pick Paracetamol?
faqs.a: Occasional mild pain; can't tolerate NSAIDs; on blood thinners.

faqs.q: When would you pick Ibuprofen (oral NSAID)?
faqs.a: Inflammation-driven pain (RA, gout, PsA flares); short-term use only.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Neither replaces exercise, weight management or DMARDs for inflammatory arthritis. Never combine oral NSAIDs with aspirin without medical advice.

/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.title: Topical NSAID Gel vs Oral NSAID: Which Is Safer?
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.description: For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends topical NSAID gels as first-line — they work almost as well as oral NSAIDs for pain but with a fraction...
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.breadcrumb: Topical NSAID Gel vs Oral NSAID: Which Is Safer?
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.question: Is topical ibuprofen gel as good as oral ibuprofen for arthritis?
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.answer: For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends topical NSAID gels as first-line — they work almost as well as oral NSAIDs for pain but with a fraction of the stomach, kidney and cardiovascular risk. Oral NSAIDs remain useful for deep joints (hip, spine) or widespread inflammation but should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time.

faqs.q: When would you pick Topical NSAID gel?
faqs.a: Hand or knee OA; localised joint pain; older adults; anyone on multiple medications.

faqs.q: When would you pick Oral NSAID (tablets)?
faqs.a: Hip/spine OA; inflammatory arthritis flares; short bursts under GP supervision.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Topical NSAIDs still carry a small systemic absorption risk — avoid on broken skin and follow the pack instructions.

/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.title: Physiotherapy vs Surgery for Knee Arthritis
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.description: NICE requires that all people with knee OA are offered a structured exercise and physio programme first — surgery (partial or total knee replacement) is a la...
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.breadcrumb: Physiotherapy vs Surgery for Knee Arthritis
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.question: Should I have physio or knee surgery for arthritis?
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.answer: NICE requires that all people with knee OA are offered a structured exercise and physio programme first — surgery (partial or total knee replacement) is a last-resort option when pain and function haven't improved despite consistent physio, weight management, and pain relief. Around 100,000 knee replacements are done in the UK each year, and outcomes are best for those who've maintained muscle strength through physio beforehand.

faqs.q: When would you pick Physiotherapy-led exercise programme?
faqs.a: First-line for everyone with knee OA; before considering surgery; for maintenance long-term.

faqs.q: When would you pick Knee replacement surgery?
faqs.a: Severe daily pain despite 12+ weeks of physio; night pain that disturbs sleep; imaging shows advanced bone-on-bone changes.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Even after surgery, physiotherapy is essential for recovery — muscle strength before surgery predicts recovery speed.

/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.title: NHS vs Private Rheumatology in the UK
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.description: NHS rheumatology provides the same specialist care and drugs as private, at no cost — but waiting times for a first appointment can be 12-30 weeks. Private c...
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.breadcrumb: NHS vs Private Rheumatology in the UK
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.question: Should I go private for arthritis care in the UK?
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.answer: NHS rheumatology provides the same specialist care and drugs as private, at no cost — but waiting times for a first appointment can be 12-30 weeks. Private consultations (£150-300) get you seen within days, but ongoing NHS care is usually still the destination for DMARDs and biologics because private prescriptions are expensive. A common practical route: private consultation to get diagnosed and started faster, then transfer to NHS for long-term treatment.

faqs.q: When would you pick NHS rheumatology?
faqs.a: Long-term treatment; DMARDs and biologics (very expensive privately); ongoing follow-up.

faqs.q: When would you pick Private rheumatology?
faqs.a: Urgent diagnosis; second opinion; you can't wait 3-6 months for a first appointment.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Ask any private consultant whether they also work in the NHS — many do, and this makes NHS transfer smoother.

/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.title: Swimming vs Walking for Arthritis
/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.description: Both are excellent, but they target different needs. Swimming and aqua aerobics remove weight from joints, making them ideal for severe knee/hip pain, flares...
/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.question: Is swimming or walking better for arthritis?
/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.answer: Both are excellent, but they target different needs. Swimming and aqua aerobics remove weight from joints, making them ideal for severe knee/hip pain, flares, or people who can't walk far. Walking is weight-bearing (better for bone density), free, and easier to fit into daily life. Most rheumatologists recommend both: walking daily for cardiovascular and bone health, swimming 1-2x/week for joint relief.

faqs.q: When would you pick Swimming / aqua aerobics?
faqs.a: Severe knee or hip OA; flares; obesity; loss of confidence; heat helps your joints.

faqs.q: When would you pick Walking?
faqs.a: Bone density (weight-bearing); daily habit; mild to moderate arthritis; free.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Cold pools can trigger some conditions (Raynaud's, fibromyalgia) — look for a heated pool.

/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.title: Yoga vs Pilates for Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.description: Both improve mobility and pain, but Pilates is generally easier to modify for arthritis because it emphasises controlled, low-range movement and core strengt...
/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.question: Should I try yoga or Pilates for arthritis?
/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.answer: Both improve mobility and pain, but Pilates is generally easier to modify for arthritis because it emphasises controlled, low-range movement and core strength. Yoga is more varied — 'gentle', 'chair' or 'restorative' yoga are arthritis-friendly, but avoid Ashtanga, hot yoga, and any deep joint-loading poses. Look for an instructor with disability or older-adult experience.

faqs.q: When would you pick Pilates (mat or reformer)?
faqs.a: Core weakness; back pain; want measured, controlled progression.

faqs.q: When would you pick Yoga (gentle/chair/restorative)?
faqs.a: Stiffness; stress and mood benefits; balance work; enjoy mindfulness.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Skip any class that pushes 'no pain no gain' — arthritis-friendly practice should never sharply hurt.

/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.title: Glucosamine vs Turmeric for Arthritis
/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.description: The evidence for both is mixed. Glucosamine (with chondroitin) has modest benefit for some people with knee OA over 6+ months of use, but many trials show no...
/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.question: Does glucosamine or turmeric work better for arthritis?
/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.answer: The evidence for both is mixed. Glucosamine (with chondroitin) has modest benefit for some people with knee OA over 6+ months of use, but many trials show no effect. Turmeric (curcumin) shows more consistent anti-inflammatory effect in trials, with fewer safety concerns for most people. Neither is a substitute for exercise, weight management or prescribed medication.

faqs.q: When would you pick Glucosamine + chondroitin?
faqs.a: Knee OA; willing to try for 3-6 months; can afford £15-30/month.

faqs.q: When would you pick Turmeric / curcumin?
faqs.a: Inflammatory-type pain; wanting an anti-inflammatory food/supplement.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Turmeric can interact with blood thinners. Speak to your pharmacist if you take warfarin, DOACs or diabetes medication.

/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.title: Heat vs Cold Therapy for Arthritis
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.description: Use heat for stiff, aching joints (typical morning OA symptoms, general muscle tension) — it relaxes tissue and boosts blood flow. Use cold for acutely infla...
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.breadcrumb: Heat vs Cold Therapy for Arthritis
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.question: Should I use a heat pad or ice pack for arthritis?
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.answer: Use heat for stiff, aching joints (typical morning OA symptoms, general muscle tension) — it relaxes tissue and boosts blood flow. Use cold for acutely inflamed, swollen joints (gout attacks, RA flares, after over-doing exercise) — it reduces swelling and dulls pain. Both are safe, cheap and evidence-supported. Apply for 15-20 minutes with a cloth barrier.

faqs.q: When would you pick Heat (heat pad, warm bath, wheat bag)?
faqs.a: Morning stiffness; ongoing dull ache; before exercise; muscle tension around a joint.

faqs.q: When would you pick Cold (ice pack, frozen peas in a cloth)?
faqs.a: Acute flare or gout attack; visibly swollen joint; after over-exertion.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never apply either directly to skin — always use a cloth or towel barrier.

/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.title: Walking Stick vs Crutch for Arthritis
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.description: For arthritis in one hip or knee, a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand reduces joint load by up to 25% — this is the standard NHS/physio recommendation. Crut...
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.breadcrumb: Walking Stick vs Crutch for Arthritis
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.question: Do I need a walking stick or a crutch?
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.answer: For arthritis in one hip or knee, a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand reduces joint load by up to 25% — this is the standard NHS/physio recommendation. Crutches (elbow crutches usually) are for temporary post-surgery use or for people with weakness or balance issues affecting both legs. Get sized properly: the handle should reach your wrist when you stand with your arms by your sides.

faqs.q: When would you pick Walking stick (single)?
faqs.a: Osteoarthritis in one knee or hip; occasional support; balance help.

faqs.q: When would you pick Elbow crutches?
faqs.a: Post-op recovery; bilateral weakness; when a stick doesn't give enough support.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: See a physiotherapist for correct sizing and gait — bad technique makes joint pain worse, not better.

/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.title: Rollator vs Walking Frame (Zimmer): Which Should You Choose?
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.description: A rollator (wheeled walker with brakes and a seat) is best for people who can walk short-medium distances but need support and rest — most arthritis, elderly...
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.breadcrumb: Rollator vs Walking Frame (Zimmer): Which Should You Choose?
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.question: Should I use a rollator or a walking frame?
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.answer: A rollator (wheeled walker with brakes and a seat) is best for people who can walk short-medium distances but need support and rest — most arthritis, elderly and MSK conditions. A traditional walking frame (Zimmer) is better for people who need maximum stability and don't need to travel far — usually indoors, after surgery, or with severe balance issues.

faqs.q: When would you pick Rollator (4-wheel, brakes, seat)?
faqs.a: Community mobility; longer walks; you want to sit and rest; outdoor use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Walking frame (Zimmer)?
faqs.a: Post-op stability; indoors only; severe balance issues; falls risk.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: NHS occupational therapy can assess you at home and provide the right aid free of charge — ask your GP for a referral.

/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.title: DMARDs vs Biologics for Rheumatoid Arthritis
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.description: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide) are the first-line drugs for RA and other inflammatory arthritis — cheap, ...
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.breadcrumb: DMARDs vs Biologics for Rheumatoid Arthritis
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.question: What's the difference between DMARDs and biologics?
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.answer: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide) are the first-line drugs for RA and other inflammatory arthritis — cheap, taken by mouth, and effective for the majority of people. Biologics (adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab and others) are injected or infused, target specific parts of the immune system, and are added when DMARDs alone aren't enough. NHS NICE guidance sets clear criteria for stepping up.

faqs.q: When would you pick Conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate)?
faqs.a: First-line for RA, PsA, some other inflammatory arthritis; NICE requires trying these first.

faqs.q: When would you pick Biologics (e.g. adalimumab, etanercept)?
faqs.a: When DMARDs alone don't achieve remission (usually after 3-6 months of adequate dose).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Both need regular blood monitoring. Never stop suddenly without medical advice — flare risk.

/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.title: Steroid Injection vs Hyaluronic Acid for Knee Arthritis
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.description: Steroid (corticosteroid) injections give faster, more consistent pain relief but the effect only lasts 4-12 weeks and repeated use can accelerate joint damag...
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.breadcrumb: Steroid Injection vs Hyaluronic Acid for Knee Arthritis
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.question: Should I have a steroid or hyaluronic acid injection in my knee?
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.answer: Steroid (corticosteroid) injections give faster, more consistent pain relief but the effect only lasts 4-12 weeks and repeated use can accelerate joint damage — the NHS typically limits them to 3-4 per year. Hyaluronic acid injections work more slowly but effects can last 6 months; NICE has moved away from routinely recommending them because evidence is mixed, and they're rarely offered on the NHS.

faqs.q: When would you pick Corticosteroid injection?
faqs.a: Acute flare; wanting fast relief; short-term bridge to physio or surgery.

faqs.q: When would you pick Hyaluronic acid injection?
faqs.a: You want longer-lasting relief and can access it privately (£250-500 per injection).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Neither treats the underlying arthritis — pair with exercise and weight management.

/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.title: Gout vs Pseudogout: What's the Difference?
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.description: Both cause sudden, severe joint pain and swelling from crystals in the joint, but the crystals and typical targets differ. Gout (uric acid crystals) most oft...
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.breadcrumb: Gout vs Pseudogout: What's the Difference?
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.question: How do I tell gout and pseudogout apart?
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.answer: Both cause sudden, severe joint pain and swelling from crystals in the joint, but the crystals and typical targets differ. Gout (uric acid crystals) most often hits the big toe, is linked to diet and alcohol, and is treated by lowering uric acid (allopurinol). Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystals) usually hits the knee or wrist, is more common in older adults, and isn't diet-linked — treatment focuses on managing flares.

faqs.q: When would you pick Gout (uric acid)?
faqs.a: Big toe, ankle or knee; often at night; alcohol/rich food trigger; family history.

faqs.q: When would you pick Pseudogout (CPPD)?
faqs.a: Knee or wrist; over 60; no diet trigger; sometimes triggered by illness or surgery.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: The only way to be certain is joint aspiration — a needle sample examined under a microscope for crystal type.

/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.title: Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis
/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.description: Osteoarthritis (OA) is wear-and-tear cartilage loss — most common, usually one-sided or asymmetrical, pain worse with activity, morning stiffness under 30 mi...
/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.question: What's the difference between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) is wear-and-tear cartilage loss — most common, usually one-sided or asymmetrical, pain worse with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is autoimmune — the immune system attacks joints, usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet), morning stiffness over an hour, plus fatigue. RA needs urgent rheumatology referral because early DMARDs prevent joint damage.

faqs.q: When would you pick Osteoarthritis (OA)?
faqs.a: Older, wear-related pattern; specific joints; activity-related; imaging shows joint space narrowing.

faqs.q: When would you pick Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)?
faqs.a: Symmetrical joint swelling; long morning stiffness; fatigue; blood tests show inflammation (ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: You can have both. If new symmetrical joint swelling develops, see your GP within 6 weeks — early RA treatment is time-critical.

/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.title: Arthritis vs Fibromyalgia | UK Comparison Guide
/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.description: Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-proc...
/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.question: How do I know if it's arthritis or fibromyalgia?
/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.answer: Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-processing condition — pain and tenderness spread across the body, plus fatigue, poor sleep and 'fibro fog', with normal joint examination and imaging. It's common to have both. Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is clinical, based on ACR criteria.

faqs.q: When would you pick Arthritis?
faqs.a: Localised joint pain; visible swelling; imaging changes; morning stiffness in specific joints.

faqs.q: When would you pick Fibromyalgia?
faqs.a: Widespread body pain; tenderness on touch; fatigue; sleep issues; 'fibro fog'.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Both respond to graded exercise, sleep hygiene and CBT — different medications from your GP.

/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.title: Tendonitis vs Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.description: Tendonitis is inflammation of the tendon attaching muscle to bone — pain is usually on movement, tender to touch over the tendon, and improves with rest and ...
/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.question: Is my joint pain tendonitis or arthritis?
/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.answer: Tendonitis is inflammation of the tendon attaching muscle to bone — pain is usually on movement, tender to touch over the tendon, and improves with rest and gradual loading. Arthritis pain comes from inside the joint itself — worse with weight-bearing (OA) or with inflammation regardless of use (RA), often stiff first thing. Physiotherapy assessment is the fastest way to tell them apart.

faqs.q: When would you pick Tendonitis?
faqs.a: Recent onset; specific tender point; movement-related; often after over-use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Arthritis?
faqs.a: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; swelling inside the joint; often symmetrical (RA).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: The two often coexist — arthritis around a joint can trigger tendonitis nearby.

/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.title: Bursitis vs Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.description: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a fluid sac that cushions between joints and tendons, most often in the shoulder, hip or knee. Pain is usually localise...
/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.question: Is it bursitis or arthritis?
/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.answer: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a fluid sac that cushions between joints and tendons, most often in the shoulder, hip or knee. Pain is usually localised, worse with pressure and movement in a specific direction. Arthritis pain is inside the joint. Bursitis often responds well to rest, ice, NSAIDs and a targeted injection; arthritis is a longer-term condition needing a treatment plan.

faqs.q: When would you pick Bursitis?
faqs.a: Sudden onset; tender to touch over a specific spot; pain when lying on that side.

faqs.q: When would you pick Arthritis?
faqs.a: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; imaging changes; pattern typical of OA or RA.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Repeated bursitis in the same joint can suggest underlying arthritis — worth investigating.

/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.title: Sciatica vs Hip Arthritis | UK Comparison Guide
