/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.description: Sciatica is nerve pain radiating from the lower back down the leg, often with tingling, numbness or shooting pain past the knee. Hip arthritis pain is felt i...
/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.question: Is my pain sciatica or hip arthritis?
/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.answer: Sciatica is nerve pain radiating from the lower back down the leg, often with tingling, numbness or shooting pain past the knee. Hip arthritis pain is felt in the groin, buttock or thigh, and rarely goes past the knee. Both can hurt when sitting for a long time, but a physiotherapy or GP examination can quickly distinguish them.

faqs.q: When would you pick Sciatica?
faqs.a: Shooting pain past the knee; tingling/numbness; often triggered by a specific movement.

faqs.q: When would you pick Hip osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Groin/buttock pain; stiffness putting on socks; hip movement painful on examination.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: You can have both — spinal and hip degeneration often coexist over 60.

/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.title: Physio Self-Referral vs GP Referral
/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.description: In most parts of England, Wales and Scotland you can now self-refer directly to NHS MSK physiotherapy — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and doesn't ...
/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.question: Do I need to see my GP before physiotherapy?
/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.answer: In most parts of England, Wales and Scotland you can now self-refer directly to NHS MSK physiotherapy — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and doesn't cost your GP an appointment slot. Search 'NHS physiotherapy self referral [your area]' — the online form takes ~10 minutes. If self-referral isn't available in your area, or you have red-flag symptoms (numbness, loss of bladder control, unexplained weight loss), see your GP first.

faqs.q: When would you pick Self-refer to NHS physio?
faqs.a: MSK pain (joint, muscle, back); no red-flag symptoms; you know self-referral works in your area.

faqs.q: When would you pick See GP first?
faqs.a: Red-flag symptoms; suspected inflammatory arthritis (needs blood tests/rheumatology); self-referral not available locally.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Waiting times for self-referral are usually similar to GP-referred routes — the benefit is speed of getting the referral in.

/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.title: PIP vs Attendance Allowance for Arthritis
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.description: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Attendance Allowa...
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.breadcrumb: PIP vs Attendance Allowance for Arthritis
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.question: Should I claim PIP or Attendance Allowance?
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.answer: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Attendance Allowance is for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of a disability or illness. You can't claim both. If you're already claiming PIP when you reach State Pension age, you can keep it.

faqs.q: When would you pick PIP (Personal Independence Payment)?
faqs.a: Aged 16 to State Pension age; long-term condition; help needed with daily life or getting around.

faqs.q: When would you pick Attendance Allowance?
faqs.a: Over State Pension age; need help with personal care because of arthritis or other illness.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Both are non-means-tested and don't affect other benefits. Citizens Advice offers free application help.

/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.title: Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.description: A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affect...
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.breadcrumb: Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.question: Do I qualify for a Blue Badge with arthritis?
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.answer: A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affects walking. You automatically qualify if you get the higher-rate mobility component of PIP or DLA; otherwise you can apply on 'discretionary' grounds by describing how far and comfortably you can walk. Local council disability parking bays and hospital blue-zone bays are separate schemes.

faqs.q: When would you pick Blue Badge?
faqs.a: Severe walking difficulty; qualifies for higher-rate PIP mobility; nationwide use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Local disabled parking?
faqs.a: Occasional need close to home/work; council-specific bays; supplements a Blue Badge.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Renewal is every 3 years and the fee is £10 in England, free in Wales and Scotland.

/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.title: Wet Heat vs Dry Heat for Arthritis
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.description: Wet heat (warm bath, hot shower, hydrotherapy) penetrates deeper and treats larger areas — best for widespread stiffness and multiple joints. Dry heat (heat ...
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.breadcrumb: Wet Heat vs Dry Heat for Arthritis
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.question: Is a warm bath or a heat pad better for arthritis?
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.answer: Wet heat (warm bath, hot shower, hydrotherapy) penetrates deeper and treats larger areas — best for widespread stiffness and multiple joints. Dry heat (heat pad, wheat bag, electric blanket) is easier and safer to use targeted at one joint. Both work; combine them (warm shower in the morning, heat pad on the sore knee in the evening).

faqs.q: When would you pick Wet heat?
faqs.a: Widespread stiffness; multiple joints; RA flares; feels good on your body.

faqs.q: When would you pick Dry heat?
faqs.a: One specific joint; easy daytime use; safe for people at risk of falls in the bath.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never bathe in water hotter than 40°C; test with an elbow first, especially if you have circulation issues or diabetes.

/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.title: Resistance Bands vs Weights for Arthritis
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.description: Resistance bands are gentler on joints, easier to modify, portable and cheap — the standard NHS/physio recommendation for starting strength work with arthrit...
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.breadcrumb: Resistance Bands vs Weights for Arthritis
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.question: Should I use resistance bands or weights for arthritis?
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.answer: Resistance bands are gentler on joints, easier to modify, portable and cheap — the standard NHS/physio recommendation for starting strength work with arthritis. Free weights and machines allow heavier loading and are excellent as you progress. Both build the muscle strength that protects joints; start with bands and add weights as confidence grows.

faqs.q: When would you pick Resistance bands?
faqs.a: Beginners; hand arthritis; anyone worried about pain; home use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Free weights / machines?
faqs.a: Progressing after a few months of bands; wanting heavier resistance; supervised gym setting.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: See a physiotherapist for a personalised programme — the wrong exercises can flare arthritis.

/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.title: Standing Desk vs Sitting Desk for Arthritis
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.description: Sit-stand desks (adjustable height) are much better than pure standing or pure sitting for anyone with arthritis. Prolonged sitting stiffens joints; prolonge...
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.breadcrumb: Standing Desk vs Sitting Desk for Arthritis
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.question: Is a standing desk better for arthritis?
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.answer: Sit-stand desks (adjustable height) are much better than pure standing or pure sitting for anyone with arthritis. Prolonged sitting stiffens joints; prolonged standing loads knees and hips. The evidence is that alternating every 30-60 minutes reduces back and joint pain more than either extreme. Add a good chair, foot rest, and a monitor at eye level.

faqs.q: When would you pick Sit-stand desk (alternating)?
faqs.a: Anyone with hip, knee or back arthritis; office workers with stiffness; hybrid workers.

faqs.q: When would you pick Fixed sitting desk?
faqs.a: You have severe standing pain and can't tolerate it even briefly.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Standing desks aren't a magic fix — a well-set-up sitting desk with regular movement breaks is usually better than a poorly set-up standing one.

/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.title: Mediterranean Diet vs Anti-Inflammatory Diet
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.description: The Mediterranean diet is the best-studied anti-inflammatory eating pattern — high in olive oil, oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts and legumes, low in...
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.question: Is the Mediterranean diet the same as an anti-inflammatory diet?
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.answer: The Mediterranean diet is the best-studied anti-inflammatory eating pattern — high in olive oil, oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts and legumes, low in red meat and processed food. 'Anti-inflammatory diet' is a broader marketing term that overlaps heavily. For UK arthritis patients, the practical answer is the same: follow a Mediterranean-style pattern using British supermarket ingredients.

faqs.q: When would you pick Mediterranean diet?
faqs.a: Best evidence base; sustainable long-term; supports heart, brain, joint and mental health.

faqs.q: When would you pick General 'anti-inflammatory' diet?
faqs.a: You already follow one; you're looking for specific elimination or supplement guidance.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Don't cut foods without medical advice — restrictive diets can cause nutritional gaps, especially in older adults.

/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.title: Magnesium vs Vitamin D for Arthritis
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.description: The NHS recommends most UK adults take 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily from October to March because sunlight is inadequate — this is especially important f...
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.breadcrumb: Magnesium vs Vitamin D for Arthritis
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.question: Should I take magnesium or vitamin D for arthritis?
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.answer: The NHS recommends most UK adults take 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily from October to March because sunlight is inadequate — this is especially important for bone health with arthritis. Magnesium supplementation is only usually needed if you're deficient (rare unless you have specific conditions). If in doubt, get your GP to check both with a blood test.

faqs.q: When would you pick Vitamin D (10 mcg daily)?
faqs.a: All UK adults in winter; anyone at risk of osteoporosis; steroid users.

faqs.q: When would you pick Magnesium?
faqs.a: Only if a blood test shows you're deficient, or on GP advice.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: High-dose vitamin D (>100 mcg/day) can be harmful. Stick to the NHS-recommended dose unless a doctor advises otherwise.

/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.title: Chair Yoga vs Tai Chi for Arthritis
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.description: Both are excellent low-impact options with strong evidence in older adults. Chair yoga is more accessible if standing is painful or unsafe — you can do it fr...
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.breadcrumb: Chair Yoga vs Tai Chi for Arthritis
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.question: Should I try chair yoga or tai chi for arthritis?
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.answer: Both are excellent low-impact options with strong evidence in older adults. Chair yoga is more accessible if standing is painful or unsafe — you can do it from a stable chair with no equipment. Tai chi requires standing balance but has the strongest evidence for reducing falls in older adults with arthritis (roughly 30% fewer falls in NHS-endorsed trials).

faqs.q: When would you pick Chair yoga?
faqs.a: Severe knee/hip pain; poor balance; can't stand for long; recovering from surgery.

faqs.q: When would you pick Tai chi?
faqs.a: You can stand safely; want falls-prevention benefit; enjoy a group class.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Look for instructors trained in adaptations for arthritis — search 'arthritis-adapted' or 'senior-focused'.

/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.title: Meditation vs CBT for Arthritis Pain
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.description: Both are recommended by NICE for chronic pain and help substantially. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) has the stronger evidence base for reducing pain in...
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.breadcrumb: Meditation vs CBT for Arthritis Pain
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.question: Does meditation or CBT work better for chronic arthritis pain?
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.answer: Both are recommended by NICE for chronic pain and help substantially. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) has the stronger evidence base for reducing pain interference in daily life and low mood. Mindfulness-based meditation (MBSR/MBCT) also reduces pain intensity and improves sleep. For UK residents, NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) offers both free of charge — self-refer online.

faqs.q: When would you pick CBT for chronic pain?
faqs.a: Pain is affecting mood, work or sleep; you want structured, goal-based help.

faqs.q: When would you pick Mindfulness meditation?
faqs.a: You want a self-guided daily practice; you've tried CBT already.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Free access via NHS Talking Therapies (self-refer) or Every Mind Matters. Private CBT £60-100/session.

/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.title: Cold Plunge vs Warm Bath for Arthritis
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.description: For arthritis, a warm bath is safer and better-evidenced than cold plunging. Warm water eases stiffness, relaxes muscle tension around joints, and supports g...
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.breadcrumb: Cold Plunge vs Warm Bath for Arthritis
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.question: Is a cold plunge or warm bath better for arthritis?
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.answer: For arthritis, a warm bath is safer and better-evidenced than cold plunging. Warm water eases stiffness, relaxes muscle tension around joints, and supports gentle movement. Cold plunging is trending but the evidence in arthritis is very limited, and it can trigger flare-ups in inflammatory conditions, worsen Raynaud's, and be dangerous for people with heart conditions.

faqs.q: When would you pick Warm bath / hydrotherapy pool (33-36°C)?
faqs.a: Stiffness; RA/OA; muscle tension; before or after exercise.

faqs.q: When would you pick Cold plunge (<15°C)?
faqs.a: Not recommended for most arthritis. If you want cold exposure, use targeted ice packs on inflamed joints only.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never cold plunge if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, Raynaud's, or you're pregnant, without medical advice.

/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.title: Joint Supplements vs Prescription Meds for Dogs with Arthritis
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.description: For UK dogs with arthritis, veterinary evidence supports starting with a comprehensive plan: weight management, joint-friendly exercise, and a quality supple...
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.breadcrumb: Joint Supplements vs Prescription Meds for Dogs with Arthritis
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.question: Should I give my dog joint supplements or vet-prescribed medication?
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.answer: For UK dogs with arthritis, veterinary evidence supports starting with a comprehensive plan: weight management, joint-friendly exercise, and a quality supplement (glucosamine, chondroitin, green-lipped mussel, omega-3). Prescription options like NSAIDs (meloxicam, carprofen) or Librela (an antibody injection) are added when supplements alone aren't enough — always under vet supervision, not self-prescribed.

faqs.q: When would you pick Joint supplements (Yumove, glucosamine)?
faqs.a: Mild-to-moderate signs; part of a long-term plan; alongside weight and exercise.

faqs.q: When would you pick Vet-prescribed medication (NSAIDs, Librela)?
faqs.a: Persistent limping; night pain; reduced quality of life; supplements alone aren't enough.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never give a dog human painkillers — paracetamol and ibuprofen can be fatal. Always consult your vet.

/glossary/dmard.title: DMARD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dmard.description: Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug — slows joint damage in inflammatory arthritis.
/glossary/dmard.question: What is dmard?
/glossary/dmard.answer: DMARD: DMARDs are drugs that slow the underlying disease process in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, JIA). Conventional DMARDs include methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide. Starting a DMARD within 3 months of RA symptoms significantly reduces long-term joint damage. All require regular blood monitoring.

/glossary/biologic.title: Biologic: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/biologic.description: Injected/infused drug targeting a specific part of the immune system. Biologic: Biologics are targeted immune-system drugs used when conventional DMARDs...
/glossary/biologic.question: What is biologic?
/glossary/biologic.answer: Biologic: Biologics are targeted immune-system drugs used when conventional DMARDs alone don't control inflammatory arthritis. UK NICE approves them based on disease activity scores. Examples: adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab, rituximab. They increase infection risk so vaccinations and screening are essential.

/glossary/nsaid.title: NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/nsaid.description: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen). NSAID: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but carry stomach, kidney and heart risk with...
/glossary/nsaid.question: What is nsaid?
/glossary/nsaid.answer: NSAID: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but carry stomach, kidney and heart risk with sustained use. NICE recommends topical NSAIDs first for hand/knee OA. Take with food; check with pharmacist if over 65, taking blood thinners, or with kidney/heart conditions.

/glossary/corticosteroid.title: Corticosteroid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/corticosteroid.description: Anti-inflammatory drug given as tablet, injection or infusion. Corticosteroid: Corticosteroids (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone) rapidly...
/glossary/corticosteroid.question: What is corticosteroid?
/glossary/corticosteroid.answer: Corticosteroid: Corticosteroids (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone) rapidly reduce inflammation but have long-term side effects: weight gain, high blood sugar, bone thinning, mood changes. Used short-term for flares or as targeted joint injections.

/glossary/synovium.title: Synovium: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/synovium.description: Thin lining of a joint that produces lubricating fluid. Synovium: The synovium is the thin membrane lining the inside of a joint capsule.
/glossary/synovium.question: What is synovium?
/glossary/synovium.answer: Synovium: The synovium is the thin membrane lining the inside of a joint capsule. It produces synovial fluid, which lubricates and nourishes cartilage. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the synovium, causing swelling, warmth and long-term joint damage.

/glossary/cartilage.title: Cartilage: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/cartilage.description: Smooth tissue covering the ends of bones in a joint. Cartilage: Cartilage is the smooth, tough connective tissue capping the ends of bones where they meet...
/glossary/cartilage.question: What is cartilage?
/glossary/cartilage.answer: Cartilage: Cartilage is the smooth, tough connective tissue capping the ends of bones where they meet in joints. It cushions impact and allows friction-free movement. In osteoarthritis, cartilage gradually thins and roughens; it has no direct blood supply so heals slowly.

/glossary/hla-b27.title: HLA-B27: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hla-b27.description: A gene marker linked to inflammatory spinal arthritis. HLA-B27: HLA-B27 is a genetic marker present in ~90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis, but...
/glossary/hla-b27.question: What is hla-b27?
/glossary/hla-b27.answer: HLA-B27: HLA-B27 is a genetic marker present in ~90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis, but also in ~8% of the general UK population without disease. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose disease — clinical assessment and imaging are essential.

/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.title: Rheumatoid factor | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.description: A blood antibody found in most people with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an antibody detected in roughly 70-80% of...
/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.question: What is rheumatoid factor?
/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.answer: Rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an antibody detected in roughly 70-80% of people with rheumatoid arthritis. Can also be positive in other conditions (Sjögren's, chronic infections) and in ~5% of healthy older adults, so it's diagnostic only with symptoms.

/glossary/anti-ccp.title: Anti-CCP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/anti-ccp.description: A more specific blood test for rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid...
/glossary/anti-ccp.question: What is anti-ccp?
/glossary/anti-ccp.answer: Anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor for diagnosing RA. Positive anti-CCP predicts more aggressive disease and helps rheumatologists decide on early aggressive treatment.

/glossary/esr.title: ESR: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/esr.description: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate — blood test for inflammation. ESR: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube, indirectly indicating...
/glossary/esr.question: What is esr?
/glossary/esr.answer: ESR: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube, indirectly indicating inflammation. Elevated in inflammatory arthritis, infections, and other conditions. Used alongside CRP to monitor disease activity, not for diagnosis alone.

/glossary/crp.title: CRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/crp.description: C-reactive protein — a faster blood marker of inflammation. CRP: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation.
/glossary/crp.question: What is crp?
/glossary/crp.answer: CRP: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation. Rises faster than ESR (hours vs days) and drops more quickly when inflammation resolves. Used to monitor flares and treatment response in inflammatory arthritis.

/glossary/joint-effusion.title: Joint effusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/joint-effusion.description: Fluid build-up inside a joint causing swelling. Joint effusion: A joint effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule, causing...
/glossary/joint-effusion.question: What is joint effusion?
/glossary/joint-effusion.answer: Joint effusion: A joint effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule, causing visible swelling, tightness and reduced movement. Common in OA, RA, gout, trauma or infection. May be drained (aspirated) to relieve symptoms and analyse the cause.

/glossary/crepitus.title: Crepitus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/crepitus.description: The grating or crackling sound in a moving joint. Crepitus: Crepitus is the audible or palpable grating, crackling or clicking felt when a joint moves.
/glossary/crepitus.question: What is crepitus?
/glossary/crepitus.answer: Crepitus: Crepitus is the audible or palpable grating, crackling or clicking felt when a joint moves. Common in OA and often harmless in isolation — many people over 40 have crepitus without pain. Concerning if painful or new.

/glossary/flare.title: Flare: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/flare.description: A period when arthritis symptoms suddenly worsen. Flare: A flare is a sudden or gradual worsening of arthritis symptoms — more pain, stiffness, swelling...
/glossary/flare.question: What is flare?
/glossary/flare.answer: Flare: A flare is a sudden or gradual worsening of arthritis symptoms — more pain, stiffness, swelling and fatigue — lasting days to weeks. Common triggers: stress, illness, over-exertion, weather changes, missed medication. Have a written flare plan agreed with your rheumatology team.

/glossary/remission.title: Remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/remission.description: When arthritis symptoms are absent or minimal. Remission: Remission means very low or absent disease activity, measured by symptoms and blood markers.
/glossary/remission.question: What is remission?
/glossary/remission.answer: Remission: Remission means very low or absent disease activity, measured by symptoms and blood markers. In RA, drug-induced remission is now a realistic goal with early DMARDs. Medication is usually continued even during remission to prevent flares.

/glossary/seronegative.title: Seronegative: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/seronegative.description: Arthritis with negative blood tests for RA antibodies. Seronegative: Seronegative arthritis means inflammatory joint disease without positive RF or...
/glossary/seronegative.question: What is seronegative?
/glossary/seronegative.answer: Seronegative: Seronegative arthritis means inflammatory joint disease without positive RF or anti-CCP tests. Includes AS, PsA, reactive arthritis. Diagnosis relies on clinical picture and imaging; management is similar to seropositive disease.

/glossary/enthesitis.title: Enthesitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/enthesitis.description: Inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. Enthesitis: Enthesitis is inflammation at the entheses — where tendons or ligaments attach to bone.
/glossary/enthesitis.question: What is enthesitis?
/glossary/enthesitis.answer: Enthesitis: Enthesitis is inflammation at the entheses — where tendons or ligaments attach to bone. Characteristic of spondyloarthropathies (AS, PsA) and often the first symptom (e.g. Achilles tendon pain, plantar fasciitis).

/glossary/dactylitis.title: Dactylitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dactylitis.description: Sausage-like swelling of an entire finger or toe. Dactylitis: Dactylitis is swelling of a whole digit ('sausage finger' or 'sausage toe') from combined...
/glossary/dactylitis.question: What is dactylitis?
/glossary/dactylitis.answer: Dactylitis: Dactylitis is swelling of a whole digit ('sausage finger' or 'sausage toe') from combined joint and tendon inflammation. Highly characteristic of psoriatic and reactive arthritis. Requires rheumatology assessment.

/glossary/morning-stiffness.title: Morning stiffness | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/morning-stiffness.description: Joint stiffness first thing after waking. Morning stiffness: Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes is typical of osteoarthritis.
/glossary/morning-stiffness.question: What is morning stiffness?
/glossary/morning-stiffness.answer: Morning stiffness: Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes is typical of osteoarthritis. Stiffness over an hour, especially symmetrical, points to inflammatory arthritis like RA and needs urgent GP review. Duration is a key diagnostic clue.

/glossary/osteophyte.title: Osteophyte: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/osteophyte.description: A bony spur that grows near an arthritic joint. Osteophyte: Osteophytes ('bone spurs') are bony outgrowths at the edges of joints damaged by...
/glossary/osteophyte.question: What is osteophyte?
/glossary/osteophyte.answer: Osteophyte: Osteophytes ('bone spurs') are bony outgrowths at the edges of joints damaged by osteoarthritis. Show clearly on X-rays. They can restrict movement and, in the spine, sometimes press on nerves — but many are painless.

/glossary/subchondral.title: Subchondral bone: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/subchondral.description: The bone just underneath the joint cartilage. Subchondral bone: Subchondral bone lies immediately beneath the joint cartilage.
/glossary/subchondral.question: What is subchondral bone?
/glossary/subchondral.answer: Subchondral bone: Subchondral bone lies immediately beneath the joint cartilage. In OA, it thickens ('sclerosis'), may develop small holes ('cysts') and gets damaged as cartilage thins. Changes are visible on X-ray and are diagnostic.

/glossary/pannus.title: Pannus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pannus.description: Inflamed tissue that invades and damages joints in RA. Pannus: Pannus is abnormal granulation tissue that grows in RA-affected joints, releasing enzymes...
/glossary/pannus.question: What is pannus?
/glossary/pannus.answer: Pannus: Pannus is abnormal granulation tissue that grows in RA-affected joints, releasing enzymes that erode cartilage and bone. Early effective DMARD treatment prevents pannus formation and the resulting joint damage.

/glossary/ankylosis.title: Ankylosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/ankylosis.description: Fusion of bones in a joint. Ankylosis: Ankylosis is stiffening or fusion of a joint, either bony (in ankylosing spondylitis) or fibrous.
/glossary/ankylosis.question: What is ankylosis?
/glossary/ankylosis.answer: Ankylosis: Ankylosis is stiffening or fusion of a joint, either bony (in ankylosing spondylitis) or fibrous. Untreated inflammation and immobility promote it. Prevention through medication and exercise is far more effective than reversal.

/glossary/uric-acid.title: Uric acid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/uric-acid.description: A waste product that forms crystals in gout. Uric acid: Uric acid is a natural waste product of purine breakdown.
/glossary/uric-acid.question: What is uric acid?
/glossary/uric-acid.answer: Uric acid: Uric acid is a natural waste product of purine breakdown. High blood levels ('hyperuricaemia') can crystallise in joints, causing gout attacks. Managed by lowering intake (alcohol, offal, seafood) and, when attacks recur, urate-lowering drugs (allopurinol).

/glossary/tophi.title: Tophi: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tophi.description: Chalky uric acid deposits under the skin in chronic gout. Tophi: Tophi are visible or palpable lumps of urate crystals in the skin, ears, tendons or...
/glossary/tophi.question: What is tophi?
/glossary/tophi.answer: Tophi: Tophi are visible or palpable lumps of urate crystals in the skin, ears, tendons or joints in long-standing gout. They cause deformity and joint damage. Their presence means urate-lowering therapy is essential.

/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.title: Physiotherapy triage | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.description: Assessment to decide the right care pathway. Physiotherapy triage: Physiotherapy triage is an initial assessment (often by a First Contact Practitioner in...
/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.question: What is physiotherapy triage?
/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.answer: Physiotherapy triage: Physiotherapy triage is an initial assessment (often by a First Contact Practitioner in general practice) to sort MSK problems into: self-management, physio treatment, imaging, or specialist referral. Reduces GP burden and speeds care.

/glossary/musculoskeletal.title: Musculoskeletal (MSK) | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/musculoskeletal.description: Related to muscles, bones, joints, tendons and ligaments. Musculoskeletal (MSK): 'Musculoskeletal' means anything involving muscles, bones, joints...
/glossary/musculoskeletal.question: What is musculoskeletal (msk)?
/glossary/musculoskeletal.answer: Musculoskeletal (MSK): 'Musculoskeletal' means anything involving muscles, bones, joints, tendons or ligaments. MSK conditions are the leading cause of work absence and disability in the UK, affecting around 20 million people. Most GP visits for back pain, joint pain and sports injuries are MSK.

/glossary/proprioception.title: Proprioception: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/proprioception.description: The body's sense of where its joints are. Proprioception: Proprioception is your brain's awareness of joint position without looking.
/glossary/proprioception.question: What is proprioception?
/glossary/proprioception.answer: Proprioception: Proprioception is your brain's awareness of joint position without looking. Arthritis and joint injury impair proprioception, worsening balance and falls risk. Specific balance and coordination exercises restore it.

/glossary/range-of-motion.title: Range of motion (ROM) | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/range-of-motion.description: How far a joint can move in each direction. Range of motion (ROM): ROM is the measurable extent of movement at a joint — flexion, extension, rotation.
/glossary/range-of-motion.question: What is range of motion (rom)?
/glossary/range-of-motion.answer: Range of motion (ROM): ROM is the measurable extent of movement at a joint — flexion, extension, rotation. Physiotherapists compare your ROM to normal ranges and track improvement. Regular gentle movement preserves ROM even in painful joints.

/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.title: Passive vs active movement | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.description: Someone moves your joint for you vs you move it yourself. Passive vs active movement: Passive movement is when a therapist moves your joint through its...
/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.question: What is passive vs active movement?
/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.answer: Passive vs active movement: Passive movement is when a therapist moves your joint through its range without you contracting muscles. Active movement is when you do it yourself. Both are used in arthritis rehabilitation — passive keeps joints supple; active builds strength.

/glossary/hydrotherapy.title: Hydrotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hydrotherapy.description: Exercise in a heated pool for pain relief and mobility. Hydrotherapy: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool (33-36°C).
/glossary/hydrotherapy.question: What is hydrotherapy?
/glossary/hydrotherapy.answer: Hydrotherapy: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool (33-36°C). Water reduces joint load and warmth eases pain, allowing movement that isn't possible on land. NHS access varies; some rheumatology units offer courses.

/glossary/occupational-therapy.title: Occupational therapy | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/occupational-therapy.description: Practical help adapting daily activities to your condition. Occupational therapy: Occupational therapists (OTs) help with practical daily activities —...
/glossary/occupational-therapy.question: What is occupational therapy?
/glossary/occupational-therapy.answer: Occupational therapy: Occupational therapists (OTs) help with practical daily activities — dressing, cooking, work, hobbies — using adapted techniques, aids and equipment. NHS OTs assess your home and provide equipment such as grab rails free of charge.

/glossary/nice.title: NICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/nice.description: The UK body that publishes health guidance. NICE: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) develops evidence-based guidelines for the...
/glossary/nice.question: What is nice?
/glossary/nice.answer: NICE: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) develops evidence-based guidelines for the NHS in England (and adopted by Wales/NI). Key arthritis guidelines: NG226 (OA), NG100 (RA), CG79 (RA in adults). Your care should broadly follow NICE guidance.

/glossary/pip.title: PIP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pip.description: Personal Independence Payment, a UK disability benefit. PIP: PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term...
/glossary/pip.question: What is pip?
/glossary/pip.answer: PIP: PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Assessed on functional impact, not diagnosis. Arthritis frequently qualifies; Citizens Advice offers free application help.

/glossary/attendance-allowance.title: Attendance Allowance | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/attendance-allowance.description: A UK benefit for people over State Pension age with a care need. Attendance Allowance: Attendance Allowance is a non-means-tested benefit for people over...
/glossary/attendance-allowance.question: What is attendance allowance?
/glossary/attendance-allowance.answer: Attendance Allowance: Attendance Allowance is a non-means-tested benefit for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of illness or disability. £68.10-£101.75/week (2025 rates). Doesn't require an assessment of ability to walk.

/glossary/blue-badge.title: Blue Badge: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/blue-badge.description: UK parking concession for people with severe mobility problems. Blue Badge: The Blue Badge is a UK-wide parking scheme giving concessions to people with...
/glossary/blue-badge.question: What is blue badge?
/glossary/blue-badge.answer: Blue Badge: The Blue Badge is a UK-wide parking scheme giving concessions to people with severe walking difficulty. Automatic eligibility with higher-rate PIP mobility; discretionary applications also possible. Fee £10 in England, free in Wales/Scotland.

/glossary/gp-referral.title: GP referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/gp-referral.description: When your GP refers you to a specialist. GP referral: GP referral is the standard NHS route to see a specialist (rheumatologist, orthopaedic surgeon).
/glossary/gp-referral.question: What is gp referral?
/glossary/gp-referral.answer: GP referral: GP referral is the standard NHS route to see a specialist (rheumatologist, orthopaedic surgeon). For MSK physio, many areas now allow self-referral without GP. Waiting times for rheumatology first appointment: 4-30 weeks depending on area.

/glossary/self-referral.title: Self-referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/self-referral.description: Booking NHS physiotherapy without a GP appointment. Self-referral: Self-referral means going directly to an NHS service without a GP letter.
/glossary/self-referral.question: What is self-referral?
/glossary/self-referral.answer: Self-referral: Self-referral means going directly to an NHS service without a GP letter. Common for MSK physiotherapy, IAPT/Talking Therapies and sexual health. Search 'NHS [service] self referral [your area]'. Saves both your and your GP's time.

/glossary/triple-therapy.title: Triple therapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/triple-therapy.description: Combining three DMARDs in rheumatoid arthritis. Triple therapy: Triple therapy typically means methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, an...
/glossary/triple-therapy.question: What is triple therapy?
/glossary/triple-therapy.answer: Triple therapy: Triple therapy typically means methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, an evidence-based combination for people with RA whose disease isn't controlled on methotrexate alone. Cheaper alternative to biologics with comparable outcomes for some patients.

/glossary/methotrexate.title: Methotrexate: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/methotrexate.description: The most common first-line DMARD. Methotrexate: Methotrexate is the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis and many inflammatory conditions, usually taken...
/glossary/methotrexate.question: What is methotrexate?
/glossary/methotrexate.answer: Methotrexate: Methotrexate is the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis and many inflammatory conditions, usually taken once weekly with folic acid on other days. Requires regular blood tests. Common side effects (nausea, tiredness) often improve after a few months.

/glossary/sulfasalazine.title: Sulfasalazine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/sulfasalazine.description: A conventional DMARD. Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine is a well-established DMARD used for RA and some spondyloarthropathies.. Taken as tablets.
/glossary/sulfasalazine.question: What is sulfasalazine?
/glossary/sulfasalazine.answer: Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine is a well-established DMARD used for RA and some spondyloarthropathies. Taken as tablets. Common in the UK because it's affordable and safe in pregnancy (unlike methotrexate). Can cause harmless orange discolouration of urine and skin.

/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.title: Hydroxychloroquine | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.description: A DMARD often used in mild RA and lupus. Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a well-tolerated DMARD used in lupus, mild RA and combination therapy.
/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.question: What is hydroxychloroquine?
/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.answer: Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a well-tolerated DMARD used in lupus, mild RA and combination therapy. Requires annual eye checks because of a small long-term retinal risk. Safe in pregnancy.

/glossary/leflunomide.title: Leflunomide: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/leflunomide.description: A conventional DMARD used in RA and PsA. Leflunomide: Leflunomide is an oral DMARD for RA and PsA when methotrexate isn't tolerated or effective.
/glossary/leflunomide.question: What is leflunomide?
/glossary/leflunomide.answer: Leflunomide: Leflunomide is an oral DMARD for RA and PsA when methotrexate isn't tolerated or effective. Requires regular blood monitoring and effective contraception in men and women (long half-life).

/glossary/adalimumab.title: Adalimumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/adalimumab.description: An anti-TNF biologic (brand Humira). Adalimumab: Adalimumab is a biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, used for RA, PsA, AS and other inflammatory conditions.
/glossary/adalimumab.question: What is adalimumab?
/glossary/adalimumab.answer: Adalimumab: Adalimumab is a biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, used for RA, PsA, AS and other inflammatory conditions. Self-injected every 1-2 weeks. Biosimilars are widely used in the NHS. Screening for TB, hepatitis and current infections is essential before starting.

/glossary/etanercept.title: Etanercept: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/etanercept.description: An anti-TNF biologic (brand Enbrel). Etanercept: Etanercept is a TNF-blocking biologic self-injected weekly or twice weekly.
/glossary/etanercept.question: What is etanercept?
/glossary/etanercept.answer: Etanercept: Etanercept is a TNF-blocking biologic self-injected weekly or twice weekly. Widely used in the UK for RA, PsA, AS and juvenile arthritis. NHS eligibility depends on disease activity scores (DAS28).

/glossary/infliximab.title: Infliximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/infliximab.description: An anti-TNF biologic given by infusion. Infliximab: Infliximab is a biologic given by hospital infusion every 6-8 weeks.
/glossary/infliximab.question: What is infliximab?
/glossary/infliximab.answer: Infliximab: Infliximab is a biologic given by hospital infusion every 6-8 weeks. Used in RA, PsA, AS, Crohn's and other conditions. Requires ongoing hospital appointments but effective and predictable.

/glossary/rituximab.title: Rituximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/rituximab.description: A biologic that targets B-cells. Rituximab: Rituximab depletes B lymphocytes, given as hospital infusions typically every 6 months.
/glossary/rituximab.question: What is rituximab?
/glossary/rituximab.answer: Rituximab: Rituximab depletes B lymphocytes, given as hospital infusions typically every 6 months. Used when TNF-blockers fail or aren't suitable. Requires screening for hepatitis B and monitoring for infection risk.

/glossary/tocilizumab.title: Tocilizumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tocilizumab.description: A biologic that blocks IL-6. Tocilizumab: Tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6, used in RA, giant cell arteritis and juvenile arthritis.
/glossary/tocilizumab.question: What is tocilizumab?
/glossary/tocilizumab.answer: Tocilizumab: Tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6, used in RA, giant cell arteritis and juvenile arthritis. Available as subcutaneous injection or IV infusion. Requires regular blood monitoring.

/glossary/jak-inhibitor.title: JAK inhibitor: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/jak-inhibitor.description: A newer oral targeted arthritis drug. JAK inhibitor: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are oral drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune...
/glossary/jak-inhibitor.question: What is jak inhibitor?
/glossary/jak-inhibitor.answer: JAK inhibitor: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are oral drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune signalling pathway. Highly effective in RA and PsA. UK regulators have restricted use in some groups because of cardiovascular and cancer safety data.

/glossary/das28.title: DAS28: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/das28.description: A score for measuring RA disease activity. DAS28: The Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) is used by UK rheumatology to decide treatment...
/glossary/das28.question: What is das28?
/glossary/das28.answer: DAS28: The Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) is used by UK rheumatology to decide treatment escalation. Combines tender joints, swollen joints, ESR/CRP and patient global rating. NICE thresholds determine biologic eligibility.

/glossary/acr-response.title: ACR20/50/70: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/acr-response.description: Trial-outcome measures for RA improvement. ACR20/50/70: ACR response criteria (American College of Rheumatology) measure whether patients improve 20%, 50%...
/glossary/acr-response.question: What is acr20/50/70?
/glossary/acr-response.answer: ACR20/50/70: ACR response criteria (American College of Rheumatology) measure whether patients improve 20%, 50% or 70% in RA trials. Used to compare drugs but rarely quoted directly in NHS clinics.

/glossary/gout-attack.title: Gout attack: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/gout-attack.description: A sudden onset of severe joint pain from urate crystals. Gout attack: A gout attack is sudden severe joint pain, swelling and redness, most often in the...
/glossary/gout-attack.question: What is gout attack?
/glossary/gout-attack.answer: Gout attack: A gout attack is sudden severe joint pain, swelling and redness, most often in the big toe. Peaks within 24 hours. Treated with NSAIDs, colchicine or short steroid course. Recurrent attacks need urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol).

/glossary/allopurinol.title: Allopurinol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/allopurinol.description: The main long-term urate-lowering drug for gout. Allopurinol: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production and prevents future gout attacks.
/glossary/allopurinol.question: What is allopurinol?
/glossary/allopurinol.answer: Allopurinol: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production and prevents future gout attacks. Started at low dose after the acute attack settles, titrated up over months. Target: uric acid <360 μmol/L, or <300 with tophi.

/glossary/colchicine.title: Colchicine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/colchicine.description: A drug for acute gout attacks. Colchicine: Colchicine is used for acute gout when NSAIDs aren't suitable.. Effective if started early in the attack.
/glossary/colchicine.question: What is colchicine?
/glossary/colchicine.answer: Colchicine: Colchicine is used for acute gout when NSAIDs aren't suitable. Effective if started early in the attack. Dose reduced from historical high doses because of side effects.

/glossary/uveitis.title: Uveitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/uveitis.description: Eye inflammation associated with inflammatory arthritis. Uveitis: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye's uveal tract, causing pain, redness and blurred...
/glossary/uveitis.question: What is uveitis?
/glossary/uveitis.answer: Uveitis: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye's uveal tract, causing pain, redness and blurred vision. Strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies. Any red painful eye with AS needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.

/glossary/sjogrens.title: Sjögren's syndrome | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/sjogrens.description: An autoimmune condition causing dry eyes and mouth. Sjögren's syndrome: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks...
/glossary/sjogrens.question: What is sjögren's syndrome?
/glossary/sjogrens.answer: Sjögren's syndrome: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks moisture-producing glands, causing dry eyes and mouth. Often coexists with RA and lupus. Managed with tear substitutes, saliva stimulants and immunosuppression when needed.

/glossary/raynauds.title: Raynaud's phenomenon | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/raynauds.description: Fingers/toes turning white and blue in the cold. Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's is exaggerated cold response — fingers/toes turn white, then blue, then...
/glossary/raynauds.question: What is raynaud's phenomenon?
/glossary/raynauds.answer: Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's is exaggerated cold response — fingers/toes turn white, then blue, then red. Primary Raynaud's is common and benign. Secondary Raynaud's is linked to autoimmune conditions (scleroderma, lupus) and needs specialist review.

/glossary/erythema-migrans.title: Erythema migrans: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/erythema-migrans.description: A characteristic rash of Lyme disease. Erythema migrans: Erythema migrans is the classic expanding 'bulls-eye' rash of early Lyme disease.
/glossary/erythema-migrans.question: What is erythema migrans?
/glossary/erythema-migrans.answer: Erythema migrans: Erythema migrans is the classic expanding 'bulls-eye' rash of early Lyme disease. Antibiotics started early prevent Lyme arthritis and other complications. If you develop joint pain after a tick bite and rash, see your GP promptly.

/glossary/septic-arthritis.title: Septic arthritis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/septic-arthritis.description: Bacterial infection inside a joint — a medical emergency. Septic arthritis: Septic arthritis is bacterial infection of a joint, causing severe pain...
/glossary/septic-arthritis.question: What is septic arthritis?
/glossary/septic-arthritis.answer: Septic arthritis: Septic arthritis is bacterial infection of a joint, causing severe pain, swelling, redness, warmth and fever. Requires emergency hospital treatment: joint drainage and IV antibiotics. Delay can destroy the joint within days.

/glossary/rice-protocol.title: RICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/rice-protocol.description: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation for joint injuries. RICE: RICE is the classic first-aid protocol for acute joint injury: Rest, Ice, Compression...
/glossary/rice-protocol.question: What is rice?
/glossary/rice-protocol.answer: RICE: RICE is the classic first-aid protocol for acute joint injury: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Recent evidence (PEACE and LOVE) suggests early gentle movement may be preferable to prolonged rest, but RICE remains a useful starting point.

/glossary/tens.title: TENS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tens.description: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for pain relief. TENS: TENS units deliver small electrical pulses through skin electrodes to block pain...
/glossary/tens.question: What is tens?
/glossary/tens.answer: TENS: TENS units deliver small electrical pulses through skin electrodes to block pain signals. Available from pharmacies for £20-50. Evidence in chronic arthritis pain is modest but many people find them helpful, with no side effects.

/glossary/kinesiology-tape.title: Kinesiology tape: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/kinesiology-tape.description: Elastic tape applied to joints for support. Kinesiology tape: Kinesiology tape is elastic tape applied by physiotherapists to support joints without...
/glossary/kinesiology-tape.question: What is kinesiology tape?
/glossary/kinesiology-tape.answer: Kinesiology tape: Kinesiology tape is elastic tape applied by physiotherapists to support joints without restricting movement. Evidence for specific pain relief is limited, but many people report benefit as part of a broader rehab plan.

/glossary/orthotics.title: Orthotics: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/orthotics.description: Shoe inserts to redistribute foot and joint load. Orthotics: Orthotics are custom or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that change how weight passes through the...
/glossary/orthotics.question: What is orthotics?
/glossary/orthotics.answer: Orthotics: Orthotics are custom or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that change how weight passes through the foot, ankle, knee and hip. Helpful for hallux valgus, flat feet, plantar fasciitis and some knee OA. NHS podiatry can prescribe them.

/glossary/acupuncture.title: Acupuncture: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/acupuncture.description: Traditional practice sometimes used for chronic pain. Acupuncture: Acupuncture uses thin needles at specific body points.
/glossary/acupuncture.question: What is acupuncture?
/glossary/acupuncture.answer: Acupuncture: Acupuncture uses thin needles at specific body points. NICE no longer recommends it for OA (evidence downgraded), but some people find it helpful for chronic pain as part of a broader plan. Rarely available on NHS for arthritis.

/glossary/cbd.title: CBD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/cbd.description: Cannabidiol — a cannabis compound used for pain. CBD: CBD is a non-psychoactive cannabis compound sold in the UK as an over-the-counter supplement.
/glossary/cbd.question: What is cbd?
/glossary/cbd.answer: CBD: CBD is a non-psychoactive cannabis compound sold in the UK as an over-the-counter supplement. Evidence for arthritis pain relief is preliminary. Legally sold if <0.2% THC. Not the same as prescribed medical cannabis.

/glossary/medical-cannabis.title: Medical cannabis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/medical-cannabis.description: Prescribed cannabis-based products in the UK. Medical cannabis: Medical cannabis has been legal on prescription in the UK since 2018 but is very rarely...
/glossary/medical-cannabis.question: What is medical cannabis?
/glossary/medical-cannabis.answer: Medical cannabis: Medical cannabis has been legal on prescription in the UK since 2018 but is very rarely prescribed for arthritis — usually reserved for specific licensed conditions (severe epilepsy, chemotherapy nausea, MS spasticity).

/glossary/hip-replacement.title: Hip replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hip-replacement.description: Surgery to replace a worn-out hip joint. Hip replacement: Hip replacement (arthroplasty) replaces the worn-out hip with metal, ceramic and plastic...
/glossary/hip-replacement.question: What is hip replacement?
/glossary/hip-replacement.answer: Hip replacement: Hip replacement (arthroplasty) replaces the worn-out hip with metal, ceramic and plastic components. Around 100,000 done in the UK yearly. Excellent outcomes for pain and function; modern implants last 20+ years for most.

/glossary/knee-replacement.title: Knee replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/knee-replacement.description: Surgery to replace part or all of a worn knee. Knee replacement: Knee replacement replaces the worn joint surfaces.
/glossary/knee-replacement.question: What is knee replacement?
/glossary/knee-replacement.answer: Knee replacement: Knee replacement replaces the worn joint surfaces. Total knee replacement is more common than partial. Recovery: hospital stay 1-3 days, walking with aid within weeks, full recovery 6-12 months. Physio before and after is critical.

/glossary/arthrodesis.title: Arthrodesis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/arthrodesis.description: Surgical joint fusion. Arthrodesis: Arthrodesis fuses bones in a joint together, eliminating movement to eliminate pain.
/glossary/arthrodesis.question: What is arthrodesis?
/glossary/arthrodesis.answer: Arthrodesis: Arthrodesis fuses bones in a joint together, eliminating movement to eliminate pain. Sometimes done in ankles, wrists, spine and small joints when replacement isn't suitable. Trades movement for pain relief.

/glossary/arthroscopy.title: Arthroscopy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/arthroscopy.description: Keyhole surgery to look inside a joint. Arthroscopy: Arthroscopy is keyhole surgery to diagnose or treat problems inside a joint.
/glossary/arthroscopy.question: What is arthroscopy?
/glossary/arthroscopy.answer: Arthroscopy: Arthroscopy is keyhole surgery to diagnose or treat problems inside a joint. Small incisions, thin camera. NICE no longer recommends 'clean-out' arthroscopy for OA — evidence showed no benefit — but it remains useful for specific mechanical problems.

/glossary/osteotomy.title: Osteotomy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/osteotomy.description: Surgery to reshape bone around an arthritic joint. Osteotomy: Osteotomy cuts and realigns bone to shift load onto a healthier part of the joint.
/glossary/osteotomy.question: What is osteotomy?
/glossary/osteotomy.answer: Osteotomy: Osteotomy cuts and realigns bone to shift load onto a healthier part of the joint. Sometimes used in younger patients with unilateral knee OA to delay replacement. Now less common with modern replacement techniques.

/glossary/meniscus.title: Meniscus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/meniscus.description: Cartilage disc in the knee that cushions the joint. Meniscus: The meniscus is a C-shaped cartilage disc in the knee that cushions and stabilises the joint.
/glossary/meniscus.question: What is meniscus?
/glossary/meniscus.answer: Meniscus: The meniscus is a C-shaped cartilage disc in the knee that cushions and stabilises the joint. Age-related tears are common and often symptomless. NICE recommends physiotherapy first for degenerative tears — surgery only for specific mechanical symptoms.

/glossary/labrum.title: Labrum: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/labrum.description: Cartilage rim of the hip or shoulder socket. Labrum: The labrum is the ring of cartilage around the hip and shoulder sockets, deepening the joint and...
/glossary/labrum.question: What is labrum?
/glossary/labrum.answer: Labrum: The labrum is the ring of cartilage around the hip and shoulder sockets, deepening the joint and helping stability. Tears can cause pain and clicking. Some are surgically treated but many respond to physiotherapy.

/glossary/bone-density.title: Bone density (BMD) | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bone-density.description: How mineral-dense your bones are. Bone density (BMD): Bone mineral density is measured by DEXA scan, expressed as a T-score.
/glossary/bone-density.question: What is bone density (bmd)?
/glossary/bone-density.answer: Bone density (BMD): Bone mineral density is measured by DEXA scan, expressed as a T-score. Below -1: osteopenia; below -2.5: osteoporosis. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D and, when needed, bisphosphonates maintain BMD.

/glossary/osteoporosis.title: Osteoporosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/osteoporosis.description: Low bone density that increases fracture risk. Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is silently reduced bone density until a fragility fracture happens.
/glossary/osteoporosis.question: What is osteoporosis?
/glossary/osteoporosis.answer: Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is silently reduced bone density until a fragility fracture happens. Screening after menopause or long-term steroid use. Managed with lifestyle, calcium, vitamin D and bisphosphonates (alendronic acid) if high risk.

/glossary/frax.title: FRAX score: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/frax.description: A tool that estimates 10-year fracture risk. FRAX score: FRAX is an online tool from Sheffield University that estimates your 10-year risk of hip and...
/glossary/frax.question: What is frax score?
/glossary/frax.answer: FRAX score: FRAX is an online tool from Sheffield University that estimates your 10-year risk of hip and major fracture based on age, sex, BMI, family and clinical factors. Used by NHS GPs to decide who needs bone-density scanning or treatment.

/glossary/bisphosphonates.title: Bisphosphonates: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bisphosphonates.description: Drugs that slow bone loss. Bisphosphonates: Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate, zoledronic acid) slow bone breakdown and reduce fracture risk...
/glossary/bisphosphonates.question: What is bisphosphonates?
/glossary/bisphosphonates.answer: Bisphosphonates: Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate, zoledronic acid) slow bone breakdown and reduce fracture risk in osteoporosis. Weekly tablet or annual infusion. Take on an empty stomach, stay upright 30 min. Rare jaw and thigh bone side effects.

/glossary/sarcopenia.title: Sarcopenia: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/sarcopenia.description: Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Sarcopenia: Sarcopenia is accelerated muscle loss with age, worsened by inactivity and low protein intake.
/glossary/sarcopenia.question: What is sarcopenia?
/glossary/sarcopenia.answer: Sarcopenia: Sarcopenia is accelerated muscle loss with age, worsened by inactivity and low protein intake. Reversible with resistance training and adequate protein (~1.0-1.2 g/kg/day). Contributes to falls and frailty.

/glossary/frailty.title: Frailty: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/frailty.description: A state of reduced reserve and resilience. Frailty: Frailty is not the same as ageing — it's reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to...
/glossary/frailty.question: What is frailty?
/glossary/frailty.answer: Frailty: Frailty is not the same as ageing — it's reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to setbacks. Assessed with tools like the Clinical Frailty Scale. Reversible early: strength training, protein, treating cataracts, medication review.

/glossary/cfs.title: Clinical Frailty Scale | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/cfs.description: A 9-point score used by NHS staff. Clinical Frailty Scale: The Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale rates frailty 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill).
/glossary/cfs.question: What is clinical frailty scale?
/glossary/cfs.answer: Clinical Frailty Scale: The Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale rates frailty 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Used across the NHS in hospital admissions and community care. Scores 1-3 fit; 4-5 vulnerable; 6+ frail.

/glossary/otago.title: Otago exercise programme | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/otago.description: An NHS-endorsed strength and balance course. Otago exercise programme: The Otago Exercise Programme is a physiotherapy-designed home programme of leg...
/glossary/otago.question: What is otago exercise programme?
/glossary/otago.answer: Otago exercise programme: The Otago Exercise Programme is a physiotherapy-designed home programme of leg strength and balance exercises. Randomised trial evidence shows ~35% fewer falls in older adults. Available through NHS falls services.

/glossary/falls-risk.title: Falls risk: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/falls-risk.description: Likelihood of falling in the next year. Falls risk: Falls risk in older adults with arthritis is doubled by pain, weakness, poor balance, medications and...
/glossary/falls-risk.question: What is falls risk?
/glossary/falls-risk.answer: Falls risk: Falls risk in older adults with arthritis is doubled by pain, weakness, poor balance, medications and vision. Assessed via history (previous falls, near-falls), timed-up-and-go test, and medication review. Halveable with structured intervention.

/glossary/ct-scan.title: CT scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/ct-scan.description: Computed tomography — detailed bone imaging. CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to build detailed cross-sectional bone images.
/glossary/ct-scan.question: What is ct scan?
/glossary/ct-scan.answer: CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to build detailed cross-sectional bone images. Better than plain X-ray for complex fractures and bony detail; poorer than MRI for soft tissue. Uses ionising radiation.

/glossary/mri.title: MRI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/mri.description: Magnetic resonance imaging — detailed joint imaging. MRI: MRI uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue and bone marrow in detail.
/glossary/mri.question: What is mri?
/glossary/mri.answer: MRI: MRI uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue and bone marrow in detail. Best for cartilage, ligaments, tendons and early inflammatory changes not visible on X-ray. No radiation. NHS waiting times vary.

/glossary/ultrasound.title: Ultrasound: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/ultrasound.description: Real-time imaging of joints and soft tissue. Ultrasound: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints, tendons and inflammation in real...
/glossary/ultrasound.question: What is ultrasound?
/glossary/ultrasound.answer: Ultrasound: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints, tendons and inflammation in real time. Increasingly used by rheumatologists for early RA detection and injection guidance.

/glossary/bone-scan.title: Bone scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bone-scan.description: Nuclear medicine test for bone activity. Bone scan: A bone (bone scintigraphy) scan uses a small dose of radioactive tracer taken up by active bone.
/glossary/bone-scan.question: What is bone scan?
/glossary/bone-scan.answer: Bone scan: A bone (bone scintigraphy) scan uses a small dose of radioactive tracer taken up by active bone. Used for detecting metastases, hidden fractures, complex regional pain syndrome and bone infections.

/glossary/dexa-scan.title: DEXA scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dexa-scan.description: The standard test for bone density. DEXA scan: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density at hip and spine.
/glossary/dexa-scan.question: What is dexa scan?
/glossary/dexa-scan.answer: DEXA scan: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density at hip and spine. Standard test for osteoporosis diagnosis. Low radiation dose. NHS available on GP or specialist referral.

/glossary/dass-score.title: DASS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dass-score.description: Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale. DASS: DASS is a self-report questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and stress.
/glossary/dass-score.question: What is dass?
/glossary/dass-score.answer: DASS: DASS is a self-report questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and stress. Used to identify mental health impact of chronic conditions like arthritis. NHS Talking Therapies uses similar tools to guide treatment.

/glossary/act-therapy.title: ACT: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/act-therapy.description: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for chronic pain. ACT: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a psychological approach for chronic pain that focuses...
/glossary/act-therapy.question: What is act?
/glossary/act-therapy.answer: ACT: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a psychological approach for chronic pain that focuses on living well with pain rather than eliminating it. Growing NICE endorsement for chronic primary pain. Available via NHS Talking Therapies.

/glossary/iapt.title: NHS Talking Therapies | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/iapt.description: Free NHS psychological therapy. NHS Talking Therapies: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) provides free CBT, counselling and mindfulness-based therapy...
/glossary/iapt.question: What is nhs talking therapies?
/glossary/iapt.answer: NHS Talking Therapies: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) provides free CBT, counselling and mindfulness-based therapy for adults with anxiety, depression and chronic pain. Self-referral online in most areas. Waiting times variable.

/glossary/nsaid-topical.title: Topical NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/nsaid-topical.description: NSAID applied as gel or cream to the skin. Topical NSAID: Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen gel, diclofenac gel) are applied to the skin over a painful joint.
/glossary/nsaid-topical.question: What is topical nsaid?
/glossary/nsaid-topical.answer: Topical NSAID: Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen gel, diclofenac gel) are applied to the skin over a painful joint. NICE first-line for hand and knee OA — comparable pain relief to oral NSAIDs but far lower systemic risk.

/glossary/capsaicin.title: Capsaicin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/capsaicin.description: A chilli-derived topical pain cream. Capsaicin: Capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) desensitises pain nerves over 2-4 weeks of regular application.
/glossary/capsaicin.question: What is capsaicin?
/glossary/capsaicin.answer: Capsaicin: Capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) desensitises pain nerves over 2-4 weeks of regular application. NICE-recommended for OA hand and knee. Available on NHS prescription. Wash hands after use.

/glossary/amitriptyline.title: Amitriptyline: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/amitriptyline.description: A low-dose antidepressant used for pain and sleep. Amitriptyline: Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25 mg at night) is a common NHS prescription for chronic pain...
/glossary/amitriptyline.question: What is amitriptyline?
/glossary/amitriptyline.answer: Amitriptyline: Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25 mg at night) is a common NHS prescription for chronic pain including fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain. Improves sleep and reduces pain sensitivity. Not addictive but takes weeks to work.

/glossary/pregabalin.title: Pregabalin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pregabalin.description: A drug for nerve pain and fibromyalgia. Pregabalin: Pregabalin (Lyrica) is used for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia.
/glossary/pregabalin.question: What is pregabalin?
/glossary/pregabalin.answer: Pregabalin: Pregabalin (Lyrica) is used for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia. Controlled drug in UK — slow to increase, slow to reduce. Side effects: drowsiness, weight gain, dependence risk.

/glossary/gabapentin.title: Gabapentin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/gabapentin.description: Related nerve-pain medication. Gabapentin: Gabapentin has similar uses to pregabalin (nerve pain, fibromyalgia).. Also a controlled drug in the UK.
/glossary/gabapentin.question: What is gabapentin?
/glossary/gabapentin.answer: Gabapentin: Gabapentin has similar uses to pregabalin (nerve pain, fibromyalgia). Also a controlled drug in the UK. Cheaper than pregabalin. Titrated up over weeks; withdrawal must be gradual.

/glossary/codeine.title: Codeine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/codeine.description: A mild opioid painkiller. Codeine: Codeine is a weak opioid, often combined with paracetamol (co-codamol).
/glossary/codeine.question: What is codeine?
/glossary/codeine.answer: Codeine: Codeine is a weak opioid, often combined with paracetamol (co-codamol). Constipation is universal; addiction risk with regular use. NICE increasingly cautions against long-term opioid use in chronic non-cancer pain.

/glossary/tramadol.title: Tramadol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tramadol.description: A moderate-strength painkiller. Tramadol: Tramadol is a controlled painkiller for moderate pain.
/glossary/tramadol.question: What is tramadol?
/glossary/tramadol.answer: Tramadol: Tramadol is a controlled painkiller for moderate pain. Interacts with many antidepressants and can lower seizure threshold. Long-term use in chronic pain is discouraged by current NHS guidance.

/glossary/morphine.title: Morphine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/morphine.description: A strong opioid, rarely used long-term in arthritis. Morphine: Strong opioids like morphine are rarely used in chronic arthritis because evidence for...
/glossary/morphine.question: What is morphine?
/glossary/morphine.answer: Morphine: Strong opioids like morphine are rarely used in chronic arthritis because evidence for long-term benefit is poor and risks (dependence, falls, respiratory depression) are high. Occasionally used short-term for severe flares or post-op.

/glossary/epidural.title: Epidural: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/epidural.description: Injection of drugs into the spinal space. Epidural: Epidural steroid injections deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to the spine for radiculopathy (nerve root...
/glossary/epidural.question: What is epidural?
/glossary/epidural.answer: Epidural: Epidural steroid injections deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to the spine for radiculopathy (nerve root pain). NICE recommends caution — some benefit for acute severe sciatica, limited role in chronic back pain.

/glossary/facet-joint-injection.title: Facet joint injection | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/facet-joint-injection.description: Steroid injection into small spine joints. Facet joint injection: Facet joint injections deliver local anaesthetic and steroid to the small joints at the...
/glossary/facet-joint-injection.question: What is facet joint injection?
/glossary/facet-joint-injection.answer: Facet joint injection: Facet joint injections deliver local anaesthetic and steroid to the small joints at the back of the spine. Used for suspected facet-mediated back pain. Evidence for lasting benefit is mixed.

/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.title: Radiofrequency denervation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.description: Nerve ablation for chronic back pain. Radiofrequency denervation: Radiofrequency denervation heats specific nerves to disrupt pain signals from spinal...
/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.question: What is radiofrequency denervation?
/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.answer: Radiofrequency denervation: Radiofrequency denervation heats specific nerves to disrupt pain signals from spinal facet joints. Considered by NICE for carefully selected patients with confirmed facet-joint pain who haven't responded to other treatments.

/glossary/spinal-fusion.title: Spinal fusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/spinal-fusion.description: Surgery joining two or more vertebrae together. Spinal fusion: Spinal fusion joins two or more vertebrae together to stop movement causing pain.
/glossary/spinal-fusion.question: What is spinal fusion?
/glossary/spinal-fusion.answer: Spinal fusion: Spinal fusion joins two or more vertebrae together to stop movement causing pain. Considered for specific structural problems (severe instability, deformity). Not a routine treatment for chronic non-specific back pain.

/glossary/prolotherapy.title: Prolotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/prolotherapy.description: Injection of irritant solutions to promote healing. Prolotherapy: Prolotherapy injects irritant solutions (often dextrose) around tendons or joints to...
/glossary/prolotherapy.question: What is prolotherapy?
/glossary/prolotherapy.answer: Prolotherapy: Prolotherapy injects irritant solutions (often dextrose) around tendons or joints to stimulate healing. Evidence is preliminary and mixed. Not routinely available on NHS. Sometimes offered privately for chronic joint pain.

/glossary/prp.title: PRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/prp.description: Platelet-rich plasma injections. PRP: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections use concentrated platelets from your own blood to promote tissue healing.
/glossary/prp.question: What is prp?
/glossary/prp.answer: PRP: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections use concentrated platelets from your own blood to promote tissue healing. Evidence for arthritis is emerging but not strong enough for routine NHS use. Common in private sports medicine.

/glossary/stem-cell.title: Stem cell therapy | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/stem-cell.description: Experimental cell-based treatments. Stem cell therapy: Stem cell therapy for arthritis remains experimental.. Regulatory framework is tight.
/glossary/stem-cell.question: What is stem cell therapy?
/glossary/stem-cell.answer: Stem cell therapy: Stem cell therapy for arthritis remains experimental. Regulatory framework is tight. Beware of overseas clinics making strong claims. UK approved treatments are limited to specific research settings.

/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.title: Weight loss for arthritis | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.description: Losing weight to reduce joint load. Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain.
/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.question: What is weight loss for arthritis?
/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.answer: Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain. Every 1 kg lost cuts knee load by about 4 kg during walking. Combine with strength work to protect muscle mass.

/glossary/bmi.title: BMI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bmi.description: Body mass index, a rough weight-for-height measure. BMI: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared.
/glossary/bmi.question: What is bmi?
/glossary/bmi.answer: BMI: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. Rough guide only — doesn't distinguish muscle from fat. NHS categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 healthy, 25-29.9 overweight, 30+ obese.

/glossary/pain-scale.title: Pain scale (0-10) | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pain-scale.description: Numeric rating of pain intensity. Pain scale (0-10): The 0-10 numeric pain rating is used in NHS clinics to track pain over time.
/glossary/pain-scale.question: What is pain scale (0-10)?
