/glossary/pain-scale.answer: Pain scale (0-10): The 0-10 numeric pain rating is used in NHS clinics to track pain over time. 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable. Useful for consultation, less useful for diagnosis (subjective).

/glossary/das28-remission.title: DAS28 remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/das28-remission.description: A DAS28 score under 2.6 indicating minimal RA activity. DAS28 remission: DAS28 < 2.6 is the standard definition of RA remission.
/glossary/das28-remission.question: What is das28 remission?
/glossary/das28-remission.answer: DAS28 remission: DAS28 < 2.6 is the standard definition of RA remission. Achievable in around half of people on early aggressive treatment. Goal of modern RA management.

/glossary/shared-decision-making.title: Shared decision-making | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/shared-decision-making.description: Doctors and patients agreeing treatment together. Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a formal NHS approach where clinicians present options...
/glossary/shared-decision-making.question: What is shared decision-making?
/glossary/shared-decision-making.answer: Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a formal NHS approach where clinicians present options and patients contribute values and preferences to reach a treatment plan. Especially important in arthritis where multiple options fit different lifestyles.

/glossary.title: Arthritis Glossary: 110+ UK Terms Explained
/glossary.description: Free UK glossary of arthritis, MSK and rheumatology terms — DMARDs, biologics, ESR, CRP, DAS28 and more, in plain English.
/glossary.question: What arthritis and rheumatology terms should I know?
/glossary.answer: Living With Arthritis's plain-English glossary covers 110+ terms across rheumatology, musculoskeletal medicine, treatment, imaging, benefits and self-management — from DMARDs and biologics through DAS28, HLA-B27, sarcopenia and frailty. Every term is medically reviewed and linked to related conditions and guides so you can quickly understand your diagnosis, appointment letters or research articles.

/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.title: Arthritis in Dogs: Signs, Treatment & Daily Care
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.description: Around 80% of dogs over 8 show signs of arthritis. Learn the early warning signs, what your vet can offer (from supplements to Librela), and simple home chan...
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Dogs: Signs, Treatment & Daily Care
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.question: Which dog breeds get arthritis most?
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.answer: Around 80% of dogs over 8 show signs of arthritis. Learn the early warning signs, what your vet can offer (from supplements to Librela), and simple home changes that make a big difference. Dogs hide pain well. Look for: slowing on walks, hesitating at stairs or the car boot, stiffness after rest that eases with movement, licking one joint, reluctance to jump on the sofa, and irritability when touched. Limping is a late sign — by the time a dog visibly limps, arthritis is usually well established.

faqs.q: Which dog breeds get arthritis most?
faqs.a: Labradors, Golden Retrievers, German Shepherds, Rottweilers and other large breeds are most affected, plus long-backed breeds like Dachshunds. But any dog can develop arthritis, especially after joint injury or with excess weight.

faqs.q: Should I walk my arthritic dog less?
faqs.a: No — movement keeps joints healthy. Switch to shorter, more frequent, consistent walks on soft ground. Avoid ball-chasing and sudden twisting games, which spike joint load.

faqs.q: Is Librela worth it?
faqs.a: Many UK owners report significant improvement. It's a monthly vet-administered injection (roughly £50-80/month). Discuss with your vet whether your dog is a good candidate — response varies.

/pets/arthritis-in-cats.title: Arthritis in Cats: The Silent Condition
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.description: Up to 90% of cats over 12 have arthritic changes on X-ray, yet most are never diagnosed — cats mask pain superbly. Here's how to spot it and what genuinely h...
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Cats: The Silent Condition
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.question: How do I know if my cat is in pain?
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.answer: Up to 90% of cats over 12 have arthritic changes on X-ray, yet most are never diagnosed — cats mask pain superbly. Here's how to spot it and what genuinely helps. Cats don't limp the way dogs do — they modify behaviour instead. A cat with sore joints jumps less, climbs less, grooms less (look for a scurfy or matted coat over the back and hips), sleeps more, and may start missing the litter tray because climbing in hurts. Owners often put this down to 'just ageing'. It's usually pain, and it's treatable.

faqs.q: How do I know if my cat is in pain?
faqs.a: Watch behaviour, not limping: reduced jumping, less grooming, hiding more, litter tray accidents, and irritability when stroked over the back or hips are the classic signs.

faqs.q: What is Solensia?
faqs.a: A monthly antibody injection licensed in the UK for feline arthritis pain — the cat version of the dog drug Librela. Many owners see improved jumping and activity within weeks. Discuss suitability with your vet.

faqs.q: Can indoor cats get arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. Age, genetics and weight matter more than lifestyle. Indoor cats are often heavier, which increases risk.

/pets/arthritis-in-horses.title: Arthritis in Horses: Managing Joints for a Longer Ridden Life | Living With Arthritis
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.description: Degenerative joint disease is the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Early management — footcare, surfaces, warm-up and vet support — keeps hors...
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Horses: Managing Joints for a Longer Ridden Life
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.question: Can an arthritic horse still be ridden?
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.answer: Degenerative joint disease is the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Early management — footcare, surfaces, warm-up and vet support — keeps horses comfortable for years longer. Early equine arthritis shows as stiffness that improves with work ('warming out of it'), shortened stride, reluctance on one rein, bunny-hopping into canter, fidgeting for the farrier, or heat and mild filling around a joint after work. Hocks, coffin joints and fetlocks are most commonly affected.

faqs.q: Can an arthritic horse still be ridden?
faqs.a: Usually yes — appropriate, consistent, correctly warmed-up work generally helps rather than harms. Your vet can advise the right level for your horse's joints.

faqs.q: Is box rest good for arthritis?
faqs.a: Generally no. Unlike acute injuries, arthritic joints stiffen with immobility. Most arthritic horses do best with maximum turnout and steady gentle movement.

faqs.q: What age do horses get arthritis?
faqs.a: It's most common from mid-teens onward, but competition horses can show joint changes from as young as 8-10. Early management makes the biggest difference.

/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.title: Arthritis in Llamas & Alpacas: A Practical Owner's Guide
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.description: Camelids are stoic animals that hide lameness until it's advanced. Learn the subtle signs of joint disease in llamas and alpacas and the husbandry changes th...
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Llamas & Alpacas: A Practical Owner's Guide
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.question: How long do llamas and alpacas live with arthritis?
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.answer: Camelids are stoic animals that hide lameness until it's advanced. Learn the subtle signs of joint disease in llamas and alpacas and the husbandry changes that keep them comfortable. Llamas and alpacas rarely show obvious lameness until joint disease is advanced. Earlier clues: spending more time cushed (lying down), rising slowly or awkwardly, lagging behind the herd, reduced range while grazing, weight shifting at the standing rest, and reluctance on slopes or rough ground. Older animals and those with previous limb injuries are most at risk.

faqs.q: How long do llamas and alpacas live with arthritis?
faqs.a: With good management many live comfortably into their late teens or twenties. Weight control, footcare and dry footing make the biggest difference.

faqs.q: Should I isolate an arthritic alpaca?
faqs.a: No — camelids are herd animals and isolation causes significant stress. Keep them with at least one calm companion, and manage feeding so they aren't pushed off hay.

/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.title: Exercise for Arthritic Pets: Little and Often Wins
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.description: The single most common mistake owners make is weekend-warrior exercise. Here's how to build a joint-friendly movement routine for dogs, cats and horses alike
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.breadcrumb: Exercise for Arthritic Pets: Little and Often Wins
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.question: Is hydrotherapy worth it for dogs?
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.answer: The single most common mistake owners make is weekend-warrior exercise. Here's how to build a joint-friendly movement routine for dogs, cats and horses alike. Consistent, moderate, frequent movement — never boom and bust. For dogs: three short walks daily beats one long weekend hike. For cats: several short play sessions with a wand toy at ground level. For horses: daily turnout plus regular gentle ridden or in-hand work. Two days of soreness after activity means it was too much; scale back and rebuild gradually.

faqs.q: Is hydrotherapy worth it for dogs?
faqs.a: For many arthritic dogs, yes — it builds muscle that protects joints without impact. UK sessions cost £25-45; some insurers cover it on vet referral.

faqs.q: My cat won't 'exercise' — what can I do?
faqs.a: Cats exercise through play. Two or three 5-minute sessions with a wand toy kept at ground level maintain joint movement without jumping strain.

/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.title: Pet Weight & Joint Health: The Treatment Owners Control
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.description: Excess weight is the most powerful — and most fixable — driver of arthritis pain in pets. A practical guide to body condition scoring and safe weight loss fo...
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.breadcrumb: Pet Weight & Joint Health: The Treatment Owners Control
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.question: How fast should my dog lose weight?
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.answer: Excess weight is the most powerful — and most fixable — driver of arthritis pain in pets. A practical guide to body condition scoring and safe weight loss for dogs, cats, horses and camelids. In dogs, studies show weight loss of 6-9% of body weight measurably reduces lameness — an effect comparable to starting an NSAID. The mechanics are simple: less load per stride, thousands of strides per day. The same principle holds for cats, horses and camelids.

faqs.q: How fast should my dog lose weight?
faqs.a: About 1-2% of body weight per week. A 30 kg Labrador losing 300-600 g weekly will reach a 4 kg target in roughly 2-3 months.

faqs.q: What's the easiest first step?
faqs.a: Measure meals with digital scales instead of a scoop, and swap treats for part of the daily food ration or vegetables like carrot (dogs). Measuring alone typically cuts 10-20% of calories.

/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.title: Home Adaptations for Arthritic Pets: 15 Cheap Changes That Work | Living With Arthritis
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.description: Ramps, rugs, raised bowls and warm beds — small changes around the home dramatically reduce daily joint strain for arthritic dogs and cats.
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.breadcrumb: Home Adaptations for Arthritic Pets: 15 Cheap Changes That Work
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.question: What single change helps most?
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.answer: Ramps, rugs, raised bowls and warm beds — small changes around the home dramatically reduce daily joint strain for arthritic dogs and cats. Slipping on laminate or tile is both painful and dangerous for arthritic pets. Lay non-slip runners along main routes, add a mat where your pet eats and drinks, and keep claws and foot fur trimmed for grip. Toe grips (small rubber rings for dog claws) help dogs that still slip.

faqs.q: What single change helps most?
faqs.a: For dogs: non-slip flooring on their main routes. For cats: a low-entry litter tray on every floor. Both remove dozens of painful movements per day.

faqs.q: Are heated beds safe for pets?
faqs.a: Yes, if designed for pets with a thermostat and chew-safe cable. They're particularly loved by arthritic cats and thin senior dogs in winter.

/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.title: Pet Arthritis: When to See the Vet (Red Flags)
/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.description: Most pet arthritis can be managed at a routine appointment — but some signs need urgent attention. Know the difference.
/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.breadcrumb: Pet Arthritis: When to See the Vet (Red Flags)
/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.question: Is limping ever an emergency?
/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.answer: Most pet arthritis can be managed at a routine appointment — but some signs need urgent attention. Know the difference. Your pet is gradually stiffer after rest, slower on walks, jumping less, grooming less (cats), or you've noticed two or more changes on the home checks in our species guides. Gradual-onset signs suit a planned consultation where your vet can examine properly and build a stepped plan.

faqs.q: Is limping ever an emergency?
faqs.a: Sudden non-weight-bearing lameness, a hot swollen joint, or lameness with a wound or after trauma needs same-day veterinary attention. Gradual mild stiffness suits a routine appointment.

faqs.q: Can I get help with vet costs in the UK?
faqs.a: PDSA and Blue Cross offer subsidised care for owners on qualifying benefits. Many practices offer payment plans, and pet insurance often covers arthritis treatment if the policy predates the diagnosis.

/pets.title: Pets & Arthritis Hub: Dogs, Cats, Horses, Llamas
/pets.description: Free UK guides to arthritis in dogs, cats, horses, llamas and alpacas — signs, vet treatments, weight, exercise and home adaptations.
/pets.question: Can pets get arthritis?
/pets.answer: Yes — arthritis is extremely common in pets. Around 80% of dogs over 8 and up to 90% of cats over 12 show arthritic changes, and it's the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Living With Arthritis's pet hub covers signs, veterinary treatments (including Librela for dogs and Solensia for cats), weight management, joint-friendly exercise and home adaptations for dogs, cats, horses, llamas and alpacas. One rule above all: never give pets human painkillers — paracetamol and ibuprofen are toxic to dogs and cats.

faqs.q: What pets get arthritis?
faqs.a: Dogs, cats, horses, llamas, alpacas and rabbits all commonly develop arthritis, especially with age, excess weight or previous joint injury.

faqs.q: Can I give my pet human painkillers?
faqs.a: Never. Paracetamol and ibuprofen are toxic to dogs and cats — paracetamol can be fatal to a cat in one dose. Only use medication prescribed by your vet.

/diet.title: Best Arthritis Diet UK | Anti-Inflammatory Foods
/diet.description: Foods to avoid with arthritis and what to eat instead: Mediterranean eating, anti-inflammatory foods, weight management and practical UK meal ideas.
/diet.question: What is the best diet for arthritis?
/diet.answer: A Mediterranean-style pattern has the strongest evidence: plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, olive oil, nuts and oily fish twice a week, with less red and processed meat, added sugar and ultra-processed food. For weight-bearing joints, losing excess weight lowers the load through the joint. No food cures arthritis.

/guides/exercise.title: Arthritis Exercises at Home UK | Living With Arthritis
/guides/exercise.description: Free arthritis exercises at home in the UK: explore knee, hip, hand and chair routines, safe progression and practical guidance from Living With Arthritis.
/guides/exercise.question: What exercise is best for arthritis?
/guides/exercise.answer: Exercise is first-line care for osteoarthritis in the UK. Combine low-impact aerobic activity (walking, cycling, swimming), strengthening work for the muscles around the affected joint, and flexibility or balance work. Build up gradually; some discomfort that settles within 24 hours is expected and does not mean harm.

/guides/benefits-pip.title: PIP for Arthritis: Complete UK Guide (2026/27) | Living With Arthritis
/guides/benefits-pip.description: Complete UK guide to PIP for arthritis: who can claim, 2026/27 rates, how points work, the form, assessment, decisions, challenges and free help.
/guides/benefits-pip.question: Can I get PIP for arthritis in the UK?
/guides/benefits-pip.answer: PIP (Personal Independence Payment) helps with the extra costs of a long-term condition such as arthritis. It is not means-tested and you can claim while working. You score points for difficulty with 12 everyday activities: 8 points gives the standard rate and 12 the enhanced rate. In Scotland you claim Adult Disability Payment instead.
/guides/benefits-pip.bodyHtml:
Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Personal Independence Payment and the DWP benefit and pension rates 2026 to 2027. Benefit rules can change, so always check the official pages before you claim.

Arthritis can make ordinary tasks harder, slower or more painful: getting dressed, cooking a meal, washing, managing tablets or walking to the shops. Personal Independence Payment (PIP) exists to help with the extra costs that come with this. Many people with arthritis are eligible but never claim, or are turned down because their form did not show the real impact. This guide covers the whole process, from checking whether you qualify to challenging a decision, so you know what to expect at each stage.

What PIP is, and what it is not

  • It is for extra living costs if you have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability and find everyday tasks or getting around difficult.
  • It is not means-tested. GOV.UK states that the amount you get is not affected by your income or savings.
  • You can claim while working. PIP is not an out-of-work benefit.
  • It is tax free and usually paid every 4 weeks.
  • It is based on how your condition affects you, not on your diagnosis.

PIP has two parts. You can get one or both:

  • a daily living part, if you need help with everyday tasks
  • a mobility part, if you need help getting around

How much PIP is in 2026/27

PartStandard (lower) weekly rateEnhanced (higher) weekly rate
Daily living£76.70£114.60
Mobility£30.30£80.00

Source: GOV.UK PIP guide and the DWP rates publication for 2026 to 2027, checked on 10 October 2026. Adult Disability Payment in Scotland is paid at the same rates for 2026/27, according to mygov.scot.

Who can claim

According to GOV.UK, you can get PIP if all of the following apply:

  • you are 16 or over
  • you have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability
  • you have difficulty doing certain everyday tasks or getting around
  • you expect the difficulties to last for at least 12 months from when they started

You usually also need to be under State Pension age to make a new claim. If you are over State Pension age, you usually claim Attendance Allowance instead, unless you got PIP or Adult Disability Payment in the last 12 months. There are also residence rules: you usually need to have lived in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years and be living in England or Wales when you apply.

The difficulty must happen most of the time. GOV.UK explains this means you expect to have difficulty on more than half of the days over a 12-month period. For arthritis with flares, this is the most important rule to understand, and it is explained below.

England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland

Where you liveBenefitRun byKey differences
England and WalesPIPDepartment for Work and Pensions (DWP)The process described in this guide
ScotlandAdult Disability Payment (ADP)Social Security ScotlandSeparate application (online, phone or paper); its own process for consultations and challenging decisions. Same 2026/27 rates as PIP
Northern IrelandPIPDepartment for CommunitiesSeparate phone lines and processes; see nidirect

If you move between Scotland and England or Wales, GOV.UK says you must tell the relevant agency and make a new claim for the other benefit. For example, if you move from England or Wales to Scotland, your PIP stops 13 weeks after you move, so apply for ADP as soon as possible.

How the points system works

PIP is assessed against 12 activities: 10 daily living activities and 2 mobility activities. Each activity has a list of statements (called descriptors) worth different points. The PIP regulations set the thresholds:

  • 8 to 11 points in the daily living activities = standard rate of the daily living part
  • 12 points or more in the daily living activities = enhanced rate
  • The same thresholds (8 and 12) apply separately to the mobility activities
Daily living activitiesMobility activities
Preparing food; eating and drinking; managing medicines or treatments; washing and bathing; using the toilet; dressing and undressing; communicating; reading; mixing with other people; making budgeting decisionsPlanning and following a journey; moving around

The "reliably" test

This is where many arthritis claims are won or lost. The DWP assessment guide says you should only be treated as able to do an activity if you can do it reliably, which means:

  • safely, in a way that is unlikely to cause harm to you or anyone else
  • to an acceptable standard
  • repeatedly, as often as is reasonably needed
  • in a reasonable time, which means no more than twice as long as someone without your condition would normally take

So if you can get dressed, but it takes you 40 minutes and leaves you exhausted and in pain, or you can walk 50 metres once but not again that day, you should explain that.

Flares and fluctuating arthritis

The regulations look at which descriptor applies on more than 50% of days over the relevant period. If different descriptors apply on different days and none reaches 50% on its own, but scoring descriptors together cover more than half the days, the descriptor that applies for the highest proportion of days is used. In practice, describe what a typical week and month look like: how many bad days, what you can and cannot do on them, and how long flares last. A diary is the best way to show this; use our PIP evidence diary.

Painkillers, aids and timing

The assessment guide also says assessors should consider whether you can do an activity when you need to. If painkillers let you get washed and dressed soon after waking, you may not score; if you have to wait a couple of hours for them to work, a scoring descriptor may apply. Using aids such as a perching stool, long-handled sponge, grab rails or a walking stick can score points if you need them to complete an activity reliably.

Examples of how arthritis can affect each activity

ActivityThings to describe
Preparing foodLifting pans, chopping, opening packets and jars, standing at the cooker, using a perching stool, relying on a microwave
Managing treatmentsHelp with injections such as methotrexate or biologics, opening blister packs, remembering doses
Washing and bathingGetting in and out of the bath, reaching feet and back, needing a shower seat or someone nearby
Toilet needsGetting on and off the toilet, wiping, needing a raised seat or rails
DressingButtons, zips, socks, shoes, bras, how long it takes, help from another person
Moving aroundHow far you can walk reliably and repeatedly, at what pace, with what aid, and how you feel afterwards

How to claim, step by step

  1. Start the claim. In England and Wales, call the PIP new claims line on 0800 917 2222 (Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 917 2222), Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm. Or write to Freepost DWP PIP 1 asking to start a claim. In some areas you can now apply fully online; GOV.UK lets you check by postcode. Have your National Insurance number, bank details and your GP or health worker's details ready.
  2. Complete the "How your disability affects you" form. You will be sent it by post (usually within 2 weeks) or emailed a link if you applied by phone. GOV.UK says you should return it within 1 month; contact the PIP enquiry line if you need more time.
  3. Send supporting evidence with the form, such as prescription lists, care plans, clinic letters and information from people involved in your care.
  4. Attend an assessment if one is needed.
  5. Get a decision letter.

You can ask for someone to join your call or to call on your behalf (you need to be with them). You may also be able to get a home visit from a DWP officer to help with your claim; ask when you call.

Filling in the form: practical tips

  • Answer every question that applies to you, even if it seems obvious.
  • Describe a typical week, including bad days and how often they happen. Avoid describing only your best or worst day.
  • For each task, say whether you can do it safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time, and what happens if you try.
  • Mention pain, stiffness, fatigue, dropping things and falls.
  • List aids and adaptations you use or need, and help you get from other people (or need, even if you do not get it).
  • Give real examples: "On 4 or 5 days a week I cannot do up buttons or a bra; my partner helps me. Getting dressed takes me about 30 minutes and I have to sit down to rest."

Evidence that helps

  • Clinic letters from rheumatology, orthopaedics or pain services that describe your condition, treatment and its effects
  • Reports from a physiotherapist or occupational therapist describing function, aids and limits
  • Your prescription list, including injections and side effects
  • A statement from a carer, family member or friend who sees how you manage
  • A symptom and activity diary covering at least a couple of weeks

You do not need to pay for new medical reports. Send what you have and explain the gaps in your own words.

The assessment

GOV.UK says you might be invited to an assessment with a health professional if more information is needed. It can take place at an assessment centre, at your home, over the phone or by video call, and usually takes about 1 hour. You can have someone with you, such as a friend or support worker. The audio is recorded; if you do not want it recorded, contact the assessment provider using the details in your invitation letter. They may ask you to do some simple movements. Only do what you can do safely and without causing more pain, and say if something would hurt or you could not repeat it.

The decision and reviews

You will get a letter saying whether you will get PIP, the date of your first payment and when your claim will be reviewed. GOV.UK says a first award is between 9 months and 10 years, depending on whether your needs are likely to change. You keep getting PIP while a review is being carried out. Tell the PIP enquiry line straight away if your needs change, you go into hospital or a care home, or you plan to go abroad for more than 4 weeks.

If you disagree with the decision

  1. Mandatory reconsideration. Ask DWP to look at the decision again, usually within one month of the date on your decision letter. It is free.
  2. Appeal to a tribunal. If you are still unhappy, appeal to the Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within one month of your mandatory reconsideration notice. It is free and independent of DWP.

Our step-by-step PIP appeal guide explains how to build a strong challenge. In Scotland, ADP decisions are challenged through Social Security Scotland; in Northern Ireland, through the Department for Communities and The Appeals Service.

What a PIP award can unlock

GOV.UK lists extra help linked to PIP. Depending on your award, this can include:

  • a Blue Badge (in England you automatically qualify if you score 8 points or more in the "moving around" activity)
  • a vehicle tax discount or exemption
  • the Motability Scheme, if you get the enhanced (higher) mobility rate
  • a Disabled Persons Railcard, if you get either part
  • Carer's Allowance for someone who cares for you at least 35 hours a week, if you get the daily living part
  • extra amounts (disability premiums) in some means-tested benefits, and possible Council Tax and bus travel help from your council

You can get PIP at the same time as all other benefits except Armed Forces Independence Payment.

Free, independent help

These organisations give free benefits advice or information. We are not connected to them:

  • Citizens Advice (England, Wales), Citizens Advice Scotland and Advice NI for form-filling and challenges
  • Turn2us for a free benefits calculator and grants search
  • Scope and Disability Rights UK for disability benefits information
  • Your council's welfare rights service, if it has one

If you are not sure whether to apply, our guide to claiming PIP for arthritis covers eligibility in more detail.

/arthritis-waiting-list-help.question: What can I do while waiting for a rheumatology appointment?
/arthritis-waiting-list-help.answer: While you wait, check your referral has been received, track your symptoms weekly, keep active, and ask about NHS physiotherapy self-referral. In England you have a legal right to start consultant-led treatment within 18 weeks, with exceptions; Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have different rules. Contact your GP if symptoms get worse so the referral can be reviewed.
/arthritis-waiting-list-help.bodyHtml:
Checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS guide to waiting times in England, NHS inform (Scotland), GOV.WALES, My Waiting Times NI and NICE guidance. Waiting times change month to month, so always check the official pages for your area.

Your first five steps after being referred

  1. Make sure the referral has actually been made. Ask your GP surgery which service you were referred to, whether it was marked routine or urgent, and when it was sent.
  2. Book or confirm the appointment. In England, many first appointments are booked through the NHS e-Referral Service using the details in your appointment request letter. If you have not heard anything within a few weeks, contact the hospital's booking or appointments team.
  3. Check the expected wait on the official site for your nation (see below), rather than relying on word of mouth.
  4. Start a simple symptom record so you can show how things change while you wait.
  5. Keep doing what helps. Most of the treatments with the best evidence for osteoarthritis, such as exercise and weight management, do not need a hospital appointment to start.

Your waiting time rights in each UK nation

Each nation runs its own NHS, so the rules are different. This is a summary; follow the links for full details.

NationWhat the rules sayWhere to check waits
EnglandYou have a legal right to start non-urgent, consultant-led treatment within a maximum of 18 weeks from when your referral is received or your appointment is booked through the e-Referral Service. If you are likely to wait longer, you can ask to be offered a different provider.My Planned Care website
ScotlandStandards of 12 weeks for a new outpatient appointment and 18 weeks from referral to treatment, plus a legal 12-week Treatment Time Guarantee for planned inpatient and day-case treatment (such as a hip or knee replacement) once you and your clinician have agreed it.NHS inform waiting times pages
WalesThe Welsh Government target is for 95% of patients to start treatment within 26 weeks of referral, with no one waiting more than 36 weeks. Official statistics show these targets are not currently being met.GOV.WALES NHS activity and performance statistics; your health board
Northern IrelandPatients are seen in order of clinical priority (red flag, urgent or routine). There is no legal maximum wait like England's 18 weeks, and published waits for many specialties are long.My Waiting Times NI, by Trust and specialty

When the 18-week right does not apply (England)

The NHS explains that the 18-week right does not apply if you choose to wait longer, if delaying is in your best clinical interests (for example, losing weight or stopping smoking before an operation), if it is appropriate to monitor your condition for a time, if you miss appointments you chose from reasonable options, or if treatment is no longer needed.

Your clock also stops when treatment starts. That can include starting a medicine, being fitted for a device, agreeing to a period of monitoring, or receiving advice on managing your condition, not only having an operation.

Using your right to choose (England)

When a GP refers you, in most cases you have the legal right to choose which hospital or service you go to, including many private hospitals that treat NHS patients, as long as it does not cost the NHS more. You can also choose a consultant-led team that provides the treatment you need.

  • Tell your GP about your preferences at the time of referral, because they choose the shortlist of hospitals in your letter.
  • Compare waits on My Planned Care. Remember that a shorter average wait does not guarantee you will be seen sooner.
  • Think about travel. A hospital further away may be quicker, but follow-up visits, scans and physiotherapy may also be there.
  • If you were not offered a choice, raise it first with the person who referred you, then with your local integrated care board (ICB).

In Northern Ireland, Trusts point out that moving to another hospital does not always mean being seen sooner and can mean repeating tests. Ask the service before switching.

Keep a symptom record

A short weekly record is one of the most useful things you can do. It helps you notice changes, it gives your GP clear reasons to review the referral, and it makes your first specialist appointment more productive.

Each week, note:

  • pain, stiffness and fatigue, each scored from 0 to 10
  • how long morning stiffness lasts
  • which joints are swollen, hot or painful (a simple body outline works well)
  • what you could not do this week, such as walking to the shop, opening jars or sleeping through
  • medicines you took, including over-the-counter painkillers, and whether they helped
  • time off work or missed activities

Photographs of swollen joints taken on a bad day are useful, because swelling may have settled by the time you are seen.

What you can do while you wait

Keep moving

NICE says the core treatments for osteoarthritis are therapeutic exercise and, where appropriate, weight management, along with information and support. Exercise is safe for most people with arthritis and does not need to wait for a specialist. Start gently, build up gradually, and expect some aching that settles within a day or so. Our exercise hub has joint-specific routines.

Get physiotherapy

The NHS says that in many areas you may be able to get physiotherapy from NHS community musculoskeletal (MSK) services without a GP referral. Some GP surgeries also have first contact physiotherapists who specialise in bone and joint problems. Check your local NHS or GP surgery website for self-referral. If you pay privately, the NHS advises choosing a chartered physiotherapist registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC).

Use pain relief safely

Ask a community pharmacist which over-the-counter options suit you, especially if you take other medicines or have stomach, kidney, heart or blood pressure problems. NICE suggests topical NSAID gels for knee osteoarthritis and considering them for other affected joints, before trying tablets. Do not keep increasing doses on your own; if you need painkillers most days, see your GP.

Protect sleep, work and mood

  • Pace your activity across the week instead of doing everything on good days.
  • Ask about workplace adjustments or a fit note if work is affected.
  • Waiting can be stressful. If your mood is low, NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral in England. See our guide to arthritis and mental health.
  • If your arthritis affects daily living or getting around, check whether you could get benefits such as PIP or, in Scotland, Adult Disability Payment.

Prepare for surgery early

If you are waiting for a joint replacement, the waiting time is a chance to get fitter for the operation. Strengthening exercises, stopping smoking, cutting down on alcohol and managing weight, diabetes or blood pressure can all help you recover. See preparing for joint replacement.

If things get worse while you are waiting

Being on a waiting list does not mean you cannot get help in the meantime. Contact your GP surgery if:

  • pain, stiffness or swelling are clearly getting worse
  • new joints are becoming swollen or painful
  • you are struggling to work, look after yourself or sleep
  • painkillers are no longer controlling your symptoms
  • you have new symptoms such as weight loss, rashes, eye problems or feeling generally unwell

Take your symptom record. Your GP can contact the hospital, send updated information or ask for the referral to be reprioritised. For suspected inflammatory arthritis, NICE's quality standard says adults with suspected persistent synovitis affecting more than one joint, or the small joints of the hands and feet, should be referred to rheumatology within 3 working days of seeing their GP. If you think you have inflammatory symptoms, such as swollen joints and morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, say so clearly.

If you are already under a rheumatology team, use their advice line. NICE's quality standard says adults with rheumatoid arthritis who have a flare or possible side effects should get advice within 1 working day of contacting rheumatology services.

Make sure you stay on the list

  • Keep your details up to date. Tell your GP and the hospital if you move, change phone number or email.
  • Reply to letters and texts. Hospitals sometimes contact people to check they still need an appointment. If you do not reply, you may be removed.
  • Tell the hospital about dates you cannot attend, such as holidays, in advance.
  • Accept reasonable offers if you can. Turning down appointments can affect your waiting time. In Scotland, guidance says refusing two reasonable offers can lead to a clinical review and your waiting time being reset.
  • Ask to go on a cancellation list if you can attend at short notice.

Getting help with problems or delays

If you cannot get answers or you are unhappy with how your referral is being handled:

  • England: contact the hospital's Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS). You can complain to the provider or to your ICB, and then to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman.
  • Scotland: the Patient Advice and Support Service (PASS), delivered by Citizens Advice Scotland, gives free independent help.
  • Wales: Llais offers free, independent complaints advocacy.
  • Northern Ireland: the Patient and Client Council gives free independent advocacy and support.

A polite, specific message usually works better than a general complaint. Include your NHS number, the date of referral, the service and what has changed since you were referred.

Get ready for your first appointment

When the letter finally arrives, you may only have a short consultation. A little preparation helps you use it well:

  • Bring your symptom record and any photographs of swollen joints.
  • List all your medicines, including doses, over-the-counter painkillers, supplements and anything you have stopped because it did not work or caused side effects.
  • Note your family history, for example relatives with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or gout.
  • Write down your top three questions and put the most important one first. Our list of questions to ask your consultant can help.
  • Wear loose clothing so the joints that trouble you can be examined easily.
  • Bring someone with you if you can. A second pair of ears helps you remember what was said.
  • Ask what happens next before you leave: tests, results, treatment, and who to contact if you have problems.

If you need adjustments to attend, such as step-free access, an interpreter or a longer appointment, contact the clinic before the day.

Should you go private?

Some people pay for a private consultation, scan or operation to avoid waiting. This is your choice, but think it through: costs can be substantial, follow-up care and medicines may not be included, and you may need to be referred back into the NHS for ongoing treatment. Read our guide to private treatment costs in the UK before you decide.

When to get medical help urgently

Do not wait for your hospital appointment if you have:

  • sudden severe pain and swelling in one joint, a change in skin colour around it or difficulty moving it, especially if you feel unwell, hot, cold or shivery. This could be septic arthritis: ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111
  • new back pain with numbness around your bottom or genitals, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels. Go to A&E or call 999
  • a joint that suddenly becomes very deformed or you cannot bear any weight after a fall
  • chest pain, breathlessness, or a painful swollen calf. Call 999

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E.

faqs.q: How long will I wait for a rheumatology appointment?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live, the hospital and how urgent your referral is. Check the official sites: My Planned Care in England, NHS inform in Scotland, your health board and GOV.WALES statistics in Wales, and My Waiting Times NI in Northern Ireland. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently.

faqs.q: What is the 18-week rule?
faqs.a: In England you have a legal right to start non-urgent, consultant-led treatment within 18 weeks of your referral being received or booked, with some exceptions. If you are likely to wait longer, you can ask to be offered a different provider. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have different rules.

faqs.q: Should I go back to my GP while I wait?
faqs.a: Yes, if your symptoms are getting worse, new joints are affected or you are struggling with daily life or work. Take a symptom record so your GP can update the hospital or ask for the referral to be reprioritised.

faqs.q: Can I refer myself to physiotherapy?
faqs.a: In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy without seeing your GP. Check your GP surgery or local NHS website.

faqs.q: Can I change hospital to be seen sooner?
faqs.a: In England, you usually have the right to choose your hospital at referral, and to ask for a different provider if you are likely to wait more than 18 weeks. Ask before switching, as moving can sometimes mean repeating tests.

faqs.q: Who can help if my referral seems to be lost?
faqs.a: Start with your GP surgery and the hospital booking team. If you still cannot get answers, contact PALS in England, PASS in Scotland, Llais in Wales or the Patient and Client Council in Northern Ireland.

/benefits-pip.title: Benefits & PIP for Arthritis: UK Financial Help Directory
/benefits-pip.description: UK directory of financial help with arthritis: PIP and ADP, UC and ESA, carers, home adaptations, council tax, energy, health costs, travel, crisis help.
/benefits-pip.question: What financial help can I get with arthritis in the UK?
/benefits-pip.answer: If arthritis affects your daily life or work, you may be able to get disability benefits (PIP, or Adult Disability Payment in Scotland, or Attendance Allowance over State Pension age), income support (Universal Credit, ESA, Pension Credit), help for carers, grants for home adaptations, council tax reductions, energy and health cost help, and travel concessions. Rules differ across the UK nations.
/benefits-pip.bodyHtml:
Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Financial help if you're disabled, the DWP benefit and pension rates 2026 to 2027, mygov.scot, nidirect and NHSBSA. Amounts are the ones shown on those official pages on that date. Most change every April, so always check the linked page before you apply.

Arthritis can cost money: taxis when you cannot manage the bus, gadgets for the kitchen, extra heating because cold makes joints stiffer, prescription charges, or lost earnings when you have to cut your hours. Many people miss out on help because they do not know it exists, or assume they will not qualify. This directory brings together the main UK sources of financial help in one place, with a short explanation of each and a link to where you apply.

How to use this directory

  1. Start with the disability benefit that fits your age and where you live (section 1). It is not means-tested, and it often unlocks other help.
  2. Check income-related help (section 2) if you are on a low income or cannot work as much.
  3. Work through the cost areas (home, energy, health, travel) that matter most to you.
  4. Use a free benefits calculator, such as those linked from GOV.UK, and get free advice if you are unsure.

1. Disability benefits (not means-tested)

These help with the extra costs of a long-term health condition. Your income and savings do not count, and you can usually get them while working.

BenefitWho it is forWhere to apply
Personal Independence Payment (PIP)Ages 16 to State Pension age in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Based on how your condition affects 12 daily living and mobility activities. The 2026/27 weekly rates were £76.70 or £114.60 for daily living and £30.30 or £80 for mobility.GOV.UK, or nidirect in Northern Ireland
Adult Disability Payment (ADP)Replaces PIP in Scotland, run by Social Security Scotlandmygov.scot
Attendance AllowanceState Pension age or older, needing help with personal care or supervision for at least 6 months. £76.70 (lower) or £114.60 (higher) a week.GOV.UK
Pension Age Disability PaymentReplaces Attendance Allowance in Scotland, at the same two ratesmygov.scot

Our complete PIP guide explains the points, the form, the assessment and challenges. If you already get ADP when you reach State Pension age in Scotland, you stay on it.

2. Help if you are on a low income or cannot work

SupportWhat it is
Universal CreditA monthly, means-tested payment for working-age people. It can include an extra amount if a Work Capability Assessment finds you have limited capability for work and work-related activity. Since 6 April 2026, that amount has two rates for new claims.
New Style ESAFor people whose health limits work, based on National Insurance contributions rather than savings. Paid every 2 weeks.
Pension CreditTops up weekly income to £238 if single or £363.25 for a couple (2026/27), if you have reached State Pension age in England, Scotland or Wales. It can unlock other help, such as help with NHS dental and travel costs.
Statutory Sick PayPaid by your employer if you are too ill to work and meet the conditions.

See our ESA and Universal Credit guide for the Work Capability Assessment and the April 2026 changes.

3. Help for carers

  • Carer's Allowance (England, Wales and Northern Ireland): £86.45 a week in 2026/27 if you care for at least 35 hours a week for someone getting a qualifying benefit and earn no more than £204 a week after deductions.
  • Carer Support Payment (Scotland): the same weekly amount, plus the Scottish Carer Supplement and extra payments for each additional person cared for.
  • Carer's Credit: National Insurance credits if you care for at least 20 hours a week.
  • Universal Credit carer element: an extra monthly amount if you care for at least 35 hours a week.

Read our Carer's Allowance guide before claiming, as it can affect the benefits of the person you care for.

4. Home: adaptations, council tax and housing costs

HelpKey facts (checked 10 October 2026)
Disabled Facilities GrantA council grant towards adaptations such as ramps, grab rails, a stairlift, a level-access shower or a downstairs bedroom. Up to £30,000 in England, £36,000 in Wales and £25,000 in Northern Ireland. It usually depends on household income and savings over £6,000, and does not affect your benefits. Scotland does not have Disabled Facilities Grants and has its own support for equipment and adaptations: contact your council.
Council equipment and occupational therapyAsk your council's adult social services for an assessment. Simple equipment and minor adaptations may be provided.
Council Tax Disabled Band Reduction SchemeIf your home has an extra room, bathroom or space you need because of a disability, your bill may be reduced to the next band down (or 17% off if you are in Band A). Northern Ireland uses domestic rates instead, with its own disabled person's allowance.
Council Tax ReductionHelp from your council if you are on a low income or get certain benefits.
Housing costsUniversal Credit can include help with rent; Housing Benefit continues for some people, including many over State Pension age.

5. Energy and keeping warm

HelpKey facts
Warm Home DiscountA one-off £150 discount on your electricity bill, usually automatic if you get certain means-tested benefits. GOV.UK said the scheme reopens in October 2026 for winter 2026 to 2027, with eligibility based on 23 August 2026. In Scotland you may need to apply to your supplier. Not available in Northern Ireland.
Winter Fuel Payment£100 to £300 for winter 2026 to 2027 if you were born on or before 27 June 1960 and live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. HMRC takes it back if your income is over £35,000. In Scotland, see Pension Age Winter Heating Payment.
Cold Weather Payment£25 for each 7-day period of very cold weather between 1 November 2026 and 31 March 2027, paid automatically if you get certain benefits. Scotland has an annual Winter Heating Payment instead.
Priority Services RegisterA free register run by energy and water companies for people who need extra help, for example because of a disability or long-term condition. Ask your supplier.

6. Health costs

  • Prescriptions: free for everyone in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. In England, you get them free if, for example, you are 60 or over, have a valid medical exemption certificate, or get qualifying benefits. Arthritis itself is not on the medical exemption list.
  • Prescription prepayment certificate (England): on 10 October 2026, NHSBSA listed the prescription charge as £9.90 an item, and a certificate as £32.05 for 3 months or £114.50 for 12 months. It saves money if you need more than 3 items in 3 months or 11 items in 12 months. You can pay for the 12-month certificate by instalments.
  • NHS Low Income Scheme: help with prescriptions, dental, eye and travel costs if you have a low income and no more than £16,000 in savings (higher limits apply in care homes). In Northern Ireland, use form HC1.
  • Travel to hospital: help may be available through the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme if you get qualifying benefits or have an HC2 or HC3 certificate.

7. Getting around

HelpKey facts
Blue BadgeParking concessions. Rules and fees differ across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. See our Blue Badge guide.
Motability SchemeUse the higher or enhanced rate of a mobility benefit to lease a car, scooter or powered wheelchair. See our Motability guide.
Vehicle tax exemptionOne vehicle can be exempt if you get, for example, the enhanced rate of the PIP mobility part, the higher rate mobility of DLA, or the enhanced rate mobility of ADP. A 50% reduction is available with the standard rate of the PIP or ADP mobility part.
Disabled person's bus passPart of the English National Concessionary Travel Scheme if you are 'eligible disabled'. Contact your council. Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own concessionary travel schemes.
Disabled Persons RailcardDiscounted rail fares for eligible disabled people, and a companion travelling with you. Check the eligibility criteria on the railcard website.
Local transport schemesMany councils run dial-a-ride or taxi voucher schemes.

8. Work

  • Access to Work: a grant towards equipment, travel and support at work, which you do not pay back. See our Access to Work guide.
  • Reasonable adjustments: your employer's legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 (England, Scotland and Wales) or the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 (Northern Ireland).

9. VAT relief on equipment

GOV.UK says that if you are disabled or have a long-term illness, you will not be charged VAT on products designed or adapted for your own personal or domestic use. This can include some mobility aids, adjustable beds and certain adaptations to your home. You need to confirm in writing that you qualify; the supplier may give you a form. People who are elderly but not disabled, or only temporarily disabled, do not qualify.

10. Emergency and crisis help

  • Budgeting Loan or Budgeting Advance: interest-free help with essential costs such as furniture, white goods or moving, if you have been on certain benefits for 6 months (or a Budgeting Advance if you get Universal Credit). You repay it from your benefits.
  • England: many councils run local welfare or crisis support schemes. Contact your council.
  • Scotland: the Scottish Welfare Fund offers Crisis Grants and Community Care Grants through your council.
  • Wales: the Discretionary Assistance Fund offers emergency and individual assistance payments.
  • Northern Ireland: Discretionary Support offers interest-free loans or grants in an extreme or exceptional situation.
  • Charitable grants: Turn2us has a free grants search tool.

A one-page checklist

Tick off each line as you check it. Not everything will apply to you.

  • ☐ I have checked whether I can claim PIP, ADP, Attendance Allowance or Pension Age Disability Payment.
  • ☐ I have used a benefits calculator to see whether I can get Universal Credit, ESA, Pension Credit or Housing Benefit.
  • ☐ If someone helps me for 35 hours or more a week, they have looked at Carer's Allowance or Carer Support Payment.
  • ☐ I have asked my council about an occupational therapy assessment, equipment and adaptations.
  • ☐ I have asked my council about the Disabled Band Reduction Scheme and Council Tax Reduction.
  • ☐ I have joined my energy and water suppliers' Priority Services Registers.
  • ☐ In England, I have checked whether I get free prescriptions or whether a prepayment certificate would save money.
  • ☐ I have checked Blue Badge, bus pass and railcard eligibility.
  • ☐ If I work, I have asked about reasonable adjustments and Access to Work.
  • ☐ I have noted when each award is due for review or renewal.

Keep copies of every form, decision letter and piece of evidence in one folder. Many awards depend on others, so a decision letter for one benefit is often your proof for the next.

Free, independent advice

Citizens Advice, Turn2us, Scope and Disability Rights UK all provide free information, and many areas have a council welfare rights service. In Northern Ireland, Advice NI can help. We are not connected to these organisations. Be wary of anyone who charges a fee to fill in benefit forms. Help is available for free.

When to get medical help

Money stress and arthritis often feed each other. If you are struggling to afford your medicines, heating or food, tell your GP or pharmacist, who may be able to help or signpost you. Speak to your rheumatology team if your symptoms are getting worse. If you feel unable to cope, contact your GP, call NHS 111, or call Samaritans on 116 123 at any time.

/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-loss.title: Sarcopenia & Muscle Loss With Arthritis | UK Guide
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-loss.description: Evidence-based UK guide to sarcopenia for adults with arthritis: protein targets, strength training, supplements and home checks.
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-loss.question: What is sarcopenia and how is it linked to arthritis?
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-loss.answer: Sarcopenia is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Arthritis speeds it up because pain reduces activity; resistance training plus enough protein can slow or reverse the decline.
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-loss.bodyHtml:
What is sarcopenia and why arthritis speeds it up

Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of muscle mass, strength and function that typically accelerates after age 60. Arthritis speeds it up because pain and stiffness cut daily movement, so muscles around painful joints waste faster than in active peers. Weaker muscles then load joints harder — a loop that worsens both problems and raises falls risk.

In UK primary care, slower walking, weaker grip, needing both hands to rise from a chair, or unintentional weight loss are practical flags. They are not a diagnosis on their own, but they are a reason to ask your GP about strength, falls risk and physiotherapy.

Protein targets that support muscle

Many older adults eat too little protein across the day. A practical target for many people is about 1.0–1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight daily, spread over meals, unless a clinician has set a different plan (for example kidney disease). Dairy, eggs, fish, lean meat, tofu, pulses and fortified drinks all count. Pair protein with resistance work — food alone rarely reverses sarcopenia.

Strength training adapted for arthritis

Two to three short sessions a week of sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, resistance-band rows and heel raises usually beat long cardio alone for muscle. Stay below sharp joint pain; mild muscle ache the next day is normal. If a joint is hot and swollen, switch to gentle range-of-motion until the flare settles. Pool work and recumbent bikes help when weight-bearing hurts.

Supplements — what has evidence

Vitamin D (especially in UK winter), creatine and leucine-rich protein have the best support when combined with training. Supplements without strength work rarely rebuild muscle. Check with a pharmacist or GP before starting creatine or high-dose vitamin D if you take other medicines.

How this links to frailty and arthritis care

Sarcopenia sits next to frailty, falls prevention and osteoarthritis exercise programmes. See our frailty management guide and exercise hub for related UK pathways. This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice.

/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.title: Best Exercises for Arthritis | UK FAQ
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.description: Low-impact walking, swimming and gentle strength training for arthritis, with UK-safe tips for flares and progression.
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.question: What are the best exercises for people with arthritis?
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.answer: Low-impact walking, swimming and gentle strength training are ideal for most people with arthritis when progressed gradually.
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.bodyHtml:
What are the best exercises for people with arthritis?

Quick answer: Low-impact cardio (walking, swimming, cycling), light strength training two to three times a week, and daily flexibility work are the safest starting mix for most people with osteoarthritis or inflammatory arthritis. They reduce pain, protect joints and improve day-to-day function when progressed gradually.

Low-impact cardio

Aim for about 30 minutes of walking most days if tolerated, or swimming, water aerobics, cycling or an elliptical trainer. These raise heart rate without the jarring load of running. Build time before intensity. On flare days, shorten the session rather than stopping for weeks.

Strength training

Strong muscles support arthritic joints. Use light weights, resistance bands or bodyweight (wall push-ups, sit-to-stands) two to three times a week. Start light and progress slowly. Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle fatigue is expected. NICE-aligned care treats exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra.

Flexibility and stretching

Gentle yoga, tai chi and daily stretches held 15–30 seconds reduce morning stiffness and keep range of motion. Avoid forcing a hot, swollen joint to end range.

Tips for safe exercise in the UK

Warm up for five minutes, ice after if a joint swells, plan rest days between harder sessions, and consider NHS physiotherapy self-referral where available. This is general UK information, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help for a hot swollen joint with fever or sudden inability to move a joint.

/diet/mediterranean-diet-for-arthritis.title: Mediterranean Diet for Arthritis: Evidence & UK Plan
/diet/mediterranean-diet-for-arthritis.description: Does the Mediterranean diet help arthritis? What NICE and the research say, plus a UK shopping list, a sample 7-day week and medicine safety notes.
/diet/mediterranean-diet-for-arthritis.question: Does the Mediterranean diet help arthritis?
/diet/mediterranean-diet-for-arthritis.answer: A Mediterranean-style diet, rich in vegetables, fruit, beans, wholegrains, fish and olive or rapeseed oil, may modestly help some people with arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis, and is good for heart health. NICE says there is no strong evidence diet changes benefit RA, but people can be encouraged to follow Mediterranean principles. It is not a cure and does not replace medicines.

faqs.q: Does the Mediterranean diet help arthritis?
faqs.a: It may help some people, particularly with rheumatoid arthritis, but the evidence is limited. A small 12-week trial found modest improvements in disease activity and physical function, and NICE says adults with RA can be encouraged to follow Mediterranean diet principles, while explaining there is no strong evidence their arthritis will benefit. It is not a cure and does not replace medicines.

faqs.q: Is the Mediterranean diet good for osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: There is only limited research in osteoarthritis. The main dietary step NICE recommends for osteoarthritis is weight management if you are living with overweight or obesity. A Mediterranean-style pattern can be a sustainable way to support weight loss and heart health.

faqs.q: Can I follow it if I am vegetarian or vegan?
faqs.a: Yes. Beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts and seeds can replace fish and meat. Vegans need reliable sources of vitamin B12, iodine and calcium. Ask a pharmacist before taking an algae-based omega-3 or other supplement, and see a dietitian if you are unsure your diet is balanced.

faqs.q: Do I need to drink red wine?
faqs.a: No. You do not need to drink alcohol to follow the pattern. If you drink, the UK guideline is no more than 14 units a week spread over 3 or more days. If you take methotrexate, ask your rheumatology team what is safe for you.

faqs.q: Is the Mediterranean diet safe with warfarin?
faqs.a: Usually yes, but leafy green vegetables are high in vitamin K, which can affect how warfarin works. The NHS says you can still eat them, but talk to your warfarin clinic before making big changes and try to keep your intake steady.

faqs.q: How long until I notice a difference?
faqs.a: There is no guaranteed timescale. In the main RA trial, differences between groups only showed in the second half of the 12 weeks. Give it at least 3 months, keep a simple symptom record and discuss it with your healthcare team.

/diet/mediterranean-diet-for-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Checked on 10 October 2026 against NICE NG100 (rheumatoid arthritis), the NHS Eatwell Guide and Arthritis UK's eating well pages. This page is general education, not a personal diet plan.

What the Mediterranean diet actually is

The Mediterranean diet is not a strict plan with rules, points or banned foods. It is a pattern of eating based on the traditional diets of countries around the Mediterranean Sea. It is built around vegetables, fruit, beans, wholegrains, nuts and fish, with olive or another plant oil as the main fat, moderate dairy, eggs and poultry, and less red meat, processed meat and sugary or highly processed food. Herbs, garlic and spices add flavour so less salt is needed.

If that list sounds familiar, it is because it is very close to the NHS Eatwell Guide. Arthritis UK makes the same point: a Mediterranean-style diet is "very similar to the recommended diet in the UK". You do not need special products, imported ingredients or a subscription to follow it.

What the evidence says for arthritis

It is worth being honest here. The Mediterranean diet has some of the better evidence of any eating pattern for people with arthritis, but that evidence is still limited and it does not replace medicines, exercise or weight management.

Official UK guidance

  • NICE NG100 (rheumatoid arthritis): NICE tells clinicians to inform adults with RA who want to experiment with their diet that "there is no strong evidence that their arthritis will benefit", but that they "could be encouraged to follow the principles of a Mediterranean diet (more bread, fruit, vegetables and fish; less meat; and replace butter and cheese with products based on vegetable and plant oils)".
  • Arthritis UK: says research has shown that a Mediterranean-style diet is helpful for people with some types of arthritis.
  • NICE NG226 (osteoarthritis): does not recommend a specific diet. Its core treatments for osteoarthritis are therapeutic exercise and, where appropriate, weight management.

Key studies

  • A Swedish randomised trial in rheumatoid arthritis (Sköldstam and colleagues, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases, 2003) compared a Mediterranean diet with an ordinary Western diet for 12 weeks in 51 people with RA on stable medicines. The Mediterranean group had a small reduction in disease activity and better physical function and vitality. It was a small, short study.
  • A systematic review in rheumatoid arthritis (Forsyth and colleagues, Rheumatology International, 2018) found only four studies that met its criteria. It reported benefits for pain and physical function, but concluded there was not enough evidence to recommend the diet widely for preventing RA.
  • A systematic review in osteoarthritis (Morales-Ivorra and colleagues, Nutrients, 2018) found just three studies. Higher adherence was linked with better quality of life, but the authors said the evidence was limited and longer trials were needed.
  • A Cochrane review of diets for rheumatoid arthritis (Hagen and colleagues, 2009) found the effects of dietary changes, including Mediterranean diets, were uncertain because the trials were small and of low quality.

The honest summary: a Mediterranean-style diet may help some people with inflammatory arthritis a little and fits UK healthy-eating advice. It is not a cure, results vary, and you should never stop or change prescribed medicines because of a diet.

Why it is worth doing even if joint benefits are modest

The strongest reasons to eat this way are not only about joints:

  • Heart health. People with inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, have a higher risk of heart and circulatory disease. Eating more fibre, oily fish and unsaturated fats, and less saturated fat and salt, is standard NHS advice for protecting the heart.
  • Weight. For osteoarthritis, NICE says any weight loss is likely to help people living with overweight or obesity, and a filling, high-fibre pattern can make that easier. See our healthy weight guide.
  • It is flexible. Nothing is completely banned, so it is easier to keep going for years rather than weeks.

How to build a Mediterranean-style plate

A simple way to start is to use your plate as a guide, in line with the Eatwell Guide:

  • About half the plate: vegetables or salad, with fruit for dessert or snacks.
  • About a quarter: wholegrain starchy food, such as wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholewheat pasta, bulgur wheat, new potatoes with skins or oats.
  • About a quarter: protein, such as fish, beans, lentils, chickpeas, eggs, chicken or tofu.
  • A small amount of fat: olive or rapeseed oil for cooking and dressing.
  • Flavour: garlic, onions, lemon, herbs and spices instead of extra salt.

What to eat more of and less of

Eat more oftenEat in moderationEat less often
Vegetables, salad and fruit (fresh, frozen or tinned in juice or water)Cheese, yoghurt and milk (choose lower-fat and lower-sugar options where you can)Red meat such as beef, lamb and pork
Beans, lentils, chickpeas and peasEggsProcessed meat such as bacon, ham, sausages and salami
Wholegrain bread, oats, brown rice, wholewheat pastaChicken and turkeyButter, lard, ghee and cream
Oily fish such as salmon, sardines, mackerel, trout, pilchards and herringUnsalted nuts and seeds (a small handful)Sugary drinks, sweets, biscuits, cakes and pastries

Useful NHS numbers:

  • Fish: at least 2 portions a week, 1 of which should be oily. A portion is around 140g. Women who have not been through the menopause, including those trying for a baby, pregnant or breastfeeding, should have no more than 2 portions of oily fish a week. Tuna does not count as oily fish.
  • Red and processed meat: if you eat more than 90g (cooked weight) a day, the NHS recommends cutting down to 70g.
  • Salt: adults should have no more than 6g a day, around 1 level teaspoon.
  • Alcohol: the UK low-risk guideline is no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days. Wine is part of some traditional Mediterranean diets, but you do not need to drink to follow the pattern. See the medicine notes below.

If you think a particular food makes your symptoms worse, read our guide to foods that may trigger symptoms before cutting anything out. It explains how to test a suspected food safely without losing important nutrients.

A UK shopping list

Everything here is in ordinary UK supermarkets and discounters, and own-brand is fine.

  • Fresh: onions, garlic, carrots, peppers, tomatoes, salad leaves, broccoli, apples, bananas, oranges, plain yoghurt, milk, eggs and a block of feta or mature cheddar.
  • Freezer: peas, spinach, mixed vegetables, berries and fish fillets.
  • Cupboard: olive or rapeseed oil; tinned tomatoes, chickpeas, beans and lentils; tinned sardines, mackerel or salmon; porridge oats, wholewheat pasta, brown rice or bulgur wheat; wholemeal bread; unsalted nuts and seeds; dried herbs, cumin, paprika and lower-salt stock cubes.

A sample 7-day Mediterranean-style week

This is an example to show what the pattern looks like with everyday UK food. It is not a calorie-counted plan. Portion sizes depend on your age, size, activity and goals. If you have diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease, gout, a history of eating problems, unplanned weight loss or other medical needs, ask your GP for a referral to a registered dietitian for advice that fits you.

DayBreakfastLunchEvening meal
MondayPorridge with sliced banana and a spoon of seedsLentil and vegetable soup with wholemeal breadBaked salmon, new potatoes with skins, broccoli and peas
TuesdayPlain yoghurt with frozen berries and oatsWholemeal pitta with hummus, salad and a hard-boiled eggChickpea, spinach and tomato stew with brown rice
WednesdayWholemeal toast with peanut butter and an appleLeftover chickpea stewChicken and vegetable tray bake with olive oil and herbs, with bulgur wheat
ThursdayScrambled eggs with tomatoes on wholemeal toastSardines on toast with saladWholewheat pasta with tomato, courgette and bean sauce and a little cheese
FridayPorridge with grated apple and cinnamonTuna, sweetcorn and bean saladBaked white fish with roasted peppers, onions and potatoes
SaturdayYoghurt, fruit and a handful of unsalted nutsVegetable omelette with saladHomemade bean chilli with brown rice and a side salad
SundayWholemeal toast with mashed avocado or tomatoLeftover chilli in a jacket potatoRoast chicken with plenty of vegetables, gravy made with less salt, and fruit for pudding

Snack ideas: fruit, a small handful of unsalted nuts, plain yoghurt, carrot sticks with hummus, or oatcakes. For a full planner with a shopping list and batch-cooking tips, see our meal plans for arthritis.

Making it easier when your joints hurt

  • Use ready-prepared veg. Frozen chopped onions, pre-cut stir-fry packs and bagged salads save painful chopping.
  • Cook once, eat twice. Soups, stews, chilli and tray bakes reheat well. Freeze portions on a good day for a flare day.
  • Open tins safely. Ring-pull tins, an electric or lever tin opener and a jar opener reduce strain on the hands.
  • Keep a flare-day shelf of tinned fish, beans, oats and frozen veg.

Eating this way on a budget

You do not need expensive olive oil or fresh fish every day. Rapeseed oil is an unsaturated oil the NHS lists alongside olive oil and is usually cheaper. Tinned sardines, mackerel and pilchards count towards your fish portions. Dried or tinned beans and lentils are among the cheapest sources of protein and fibre, and frozen vegetables are as nutritious as fresh. If you are struggling to afford food, Citizens Advice can check whether you are getting all the help you are entitled to.

Medicines and safety notes

Changing to a Mediterranean-style diet is safe for most people, but a few points matter if you take arthritis or other medicines:

  • Warfarin: foods high in vitamin K, such as broccoli, spinach and other green leafy vegetables, can affect how warfarin works. The NHS says you can still eat them, but talk to your warfarin clinic before making big changes, and aim to keep the amount you eat fairly steady from week to week. Do not take vitamin K supplements, and avoid cranberry and grapefruit juice while on warfarin.
  • Methotrexate: alcohol and methotrexate can both affect the liver. If wine is part of your idea of a Mediterranean diet, check with your rheumatology team how much, if any, is safe for you.
  • NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen: take them with or after food as your leaflet advises. A healthy diet does not replace any stomach protection you are prescribed.
  • Diabetes medicines: large changes to carbohydrate intake can affect blood glucose. Speak to your diabetes team or GP first.
  • Kidney disease: lots of beans, nuts, tomatoes and some salt substitutes can be high in potassium or phosphate. Ask your kidney team or dietitian.

This is a food pattern, not a supplement plan. Ask a pharmacist to check any supplement, such as fish oil or turmeric, against your medicines first. Our omega-3 evidence review covers fish oil safety in detail.

Five small first steps

  1. Swap butter for an olive or rapeseed oil spread, or use oil for cooking.
  2. Add one extra portion of vegetables to your main meal each day.
  3. Have one meal with tinned or fresh oily fish this week.
  4. Replace one meat meal with beans, lentils or chickpeas.
  5. Switch white bread, pasta or rice to wholegrain versions, one at a time.

Small changes kept up for months matter more than a perfect week. Read our anti-inflammatory diet guide for how this pattern compares with other "anti-inflammatory" eating advice.

How to tell if it is helping you

Effects on joints are usually modest and slow, so keep a simple record. Once a week, score pain, stiffness and fatigue from 0 to 10, and note flares, medicine changes, sleep and activity, since these affect symptoms too. Give it at least 3 months and take your notes to your next appointment. You may also notice benefits in energy, digestion, weight or blood pressure.

When to get medical help

Diet changes should not delay medical care. Speak to your GP, rheumatology team or NHS 111 if:

  • you have a hot, red, swollen joint, especially with a fever or feeling unwell. Call 999 or go to A&E if you feel very unwell
  • your joint pain, swelling or stiffness is getting worse despite your treatment
  • you are losing weight without trying, or have lost your appetite
  • you have ongoing diarrhoea, blood in your poo, or stomach pain after changing your diet
  • you want individual advice because of diabetes, kidney disease, food allergies, coeliac disease or another condition. Ask your GP about a referral to an NHS dietitian

/blog/category/exercise.bodyHtml:
Arthritis exercise articles and guides

This category gathers evidence-based UK articles on safe exercise for arthritis — strength, mobility, low-impact cardio and joint-protective movement. Pieces are written for people managing osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis and related pain, with practical pacing tips rather than one-size gym plans.

Typical topics include walking and swimming programmes, chair and resistance-band work, what to do in a flare, and how exercise links to frailty and sarcopenia. Browse the listed posts below, or start at the main exercise hub and best exercises FAQ.

How to use these articles

  • Pick one routine you can keep for two weeks before adding load
  • Use the 24-hour rule: if a joint is clearly worse the next day, trim the next session
  • Combine movement with sleep, weight and medication plans from your NHS team

Educational information only — not a substitute for physiotherapy or medical advice.
